title: Driving Behaviour Risk Assessment

detail.title: Driving Behaviour Risk Assessment
detail.abstract: Road safety continues to be a pressing global concern, with a significant increase in road accidents and their impact on public safety and the well-being of individuals. Despite the continuous improvement in road infrastructure and advanced vehicle technology, the global challenges of road accidents remain paramount. This study delves into the critical analysis of the issue of risky driving behaviours and how they contribute to the implications for road safety through the application of a machine learning approach with the integration of various data sources. The use of both primary and secondary data acquisition sources is the key aspect of the methodology. The primary data are obtained from telematics devices installed in vehicles, providing information on driving behaviour directly from the vehicles. On the other hand, secondary data are obtained from external sources such as OpenStreetMap (OSM), which complement the primary data by providing additional environmental and contextual information related to road conditions, traffic patterns, and other relevant factors. This integrated approach allows the comprehensive analysis of driving behaviour patterns. The key objective of this study is to seek a better understanding of driving behaviour risk assessment and how it contributes to the significant development of effective road safety measures, and provides a real-time risk assessment of drivers after completing every journey. By utilising the K-Means clustering algorithm on the diverse dataset from different sources, this study aims to address risky driving behaviour of drivers and improve road management. The proposed results of this research bear a significant implication for road safety management, providing valuable insight into the efficacy of employing cutting-edge technologies and machine learning algorithms in assessing driving behaviour risks. Ultimately, by implementing a machine learning algorithm using various clustering techniques such as K-means and evaluating the result from the clustering model with the silhouette Euclidean score and the sum of squared error matrices, this study achieved the number of clusters K to be 4, which significantly denotes the classification of drivers based on their driving patterns. By examining the characteristics of the cluster, the driving performance of each driver was categorised into 4 groups, with each group representing similar driving patterns with similar driving styles. Finally, this study aims to foster safer roads for motorists and other road users by providing driving feedback on every journey completed.

title: Funding Rate Mechanism in Perpetual Futures

detail.title: Funding Rate Mechanism in Perpetual Futures
detail.abstract: This paper studies funding rates in cryptocurrency perpetual futures as an algorithmic feedback rule rather than a passive transfer. In a continuous-time equilibrium with risk-constrained arbitrageurs and momentum speculators, a linear funding rule induces an endogenous mean-reverting basis. We derive a simple stability condition and characterize a welfare-optimal feedback strength. We then analyze how the funding update interval, funding rate caps, and clamp-style piecewise-linear rules used by major exchanges affect basis volatility and funding tails. A jump-and-crisis extension with liquidation-driven crashes generates large negative basis spikes and slow recoveries.

title: Optimal Strategy and Deep Hedging for Share Repurchase Programs

detail.title: Optimal Strategy and Deep Hedging for Share Repurchase Programs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report no potential competing interests. The opinions expressed in this document are solely those of the authors and do not represent in any way those of their present and past employers.

detail.abstract: In recent decades, companies have frequently adopted share repurchase programs to return capital to shareholders or for other strategic purposes, instructing investment banks to rapidly buy back shares on their behalf. When the executing institution is allowed to hedge its exposure, it encounters several challenges due to the intrinsic features of the product. Moreover, contractual clauses or market regulations on trading activity may make it infeasible to rely on Greeks. In this work, we address the hedging of these products by developing a machine-learning framework that determines the optimal execution of the buyback while explicitly accounting for the bank's actual trading capabilities. This unified treatment of execution and hedging yields substantial performance improvements, resulting in an optimized policy that provides a feasible and realistic hedging approach. The pricing of these programs can be framed in terms of the discount that banks offer to the client on the price at which the shares are delivered. Since, in our framework, risk measures serve as objective functions, we exploit the concept of indifference pricing to compute this discount, thereby capturing the actual execution performance.

title: The Grandparent Effect: Does a New Grandchild Change How Long You Expect to Live?
affiliations: Middle East Technical University

detail.title: The Grandparent Effect: Does a New Grandchild Change How Long You Expect to Live?
detail.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of being a first-time grandparent on individuals' subjective survival probabilities. Analyses are conducted using Waves 4–6 (2011–2015) of Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe data. The Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) doubly robust difference-in-differences method, accounting for staggered treatment timing and heterogeneous effects, is applied. The findings demonstrate that the birth of the first grandchild reduces the standardized subjective survival probability by approximately 3.8 percentage points. Event study graphs show no significant difference in pre-treatment periods and reveal that the effect deepens over time. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the effect persists across broad subgroups, and the findings remain robust under alternative estimators. The results suggest that becoming a first-time grandparent triggers the internalization of the old-age identity, systematically reducing individuals' life expectations, which can have substantial implications for economic behaviors such as saving, retirement, and consumption decisions.

title: Macroeconomic Shocks and Banking Sector Asset Quality in Ghana: Evidence from VAR and Stress Testing

detail.title: Macroeconomic Shocks and Banking Sector Asset Quality in Ghana: Evidence from VAR and Stress Testing
detail.abstract: This paper examines the dynamic relationship between macroeconomic shocks and banking sector asset quality in Ghana using a Vector Autoregression (VAR) framework and scenario based stress testing. Monthly data covering key macro financial indicators, including exchange rates, inflation, monetary policy rates, GDP, and bank profitability, are analyzed to assess their impact on the non-performing loans (NPLs) ratio. Impulse response functions reveal that exchange rate shocks exert the largest and most persistent effect on NPLs, while monetary policy and inflation shocks have moderate but non-negligible impacts. GDP shocks exhibit limited influence. Stress testing under adverse macroeconomic scenarios shows that a severe currency crisis could raise the NPL ratio by more than 5 percentage points relative to current levels, highlighting significant financial stability risks. The findings underline the central role of exchange rate dynamics in credit risk transmission and provide policy-relevant insights for macroprudential regulation and financial stability oversight in emerging economies.

title: Evaluating the Relationship Between Video Game Microtransactions and Addictive Behaviours
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Evaluating the Relationship Between Video Game Microtransactions and Addictive Behaviours
detail.abstract: Microtransactions and loot boxes have become core revenue mechanisms in contemporary video games, raising policy concern that gambling-like design and frictionless payments may be associated with addictive consumption patterns and welfare-reducing outcomes. Although a growing literature links loot box spending with problem gambling severity, evidence remains mixed on the broader relationship between disordered gaming, gambling, and other compulsive spending behaviours. This paper proposes an Australian study estimating prevalence patterns and conditional associations, not causal effects, to map how microtransaction demand relates to three distinct but potentially overlapping constructs: disordered gaming, problem gambling severity, and compulsive buying. Using a cross-sectional online survey of approximately 800 Australian university students who have played video games in the past 90 days, the design measures (i) monthly microtransaction expenditure in AUD and (ii) weekly gaming hours, alongside validated scales: the Gaming Addiction Scale (GAS), the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI), and the Bergen Shopping Addiction Scale (BSAS). The primary econometric approach is a two-part model separating participation (any microtransaction spend) from conditional intensity (log(1 + spend)), supplemented by quantile regression for upper-tail spending and pre-specified robustness checks addressing non-linearity, heteroskedasticity, and influential outliers. Interaction terms (e.g., GAS × PGSI) test hypotheses about substitution versus complementarity between addictive behaviours within microtransaction demand. The papers contribution is threefold: it distinguishes monetary spending from time as separate consumption constructs, integrates compulsive buying as an additional harm channel, and directly connects empirical tests to policy debates, including Australias strengthened classification settings for gambling-like content in video games commencing 22 September 2024 [2] and the ICD-11 coming into effect [19].

title: Does Extending Working Lives Crowd Out Youth Employment? Evidence from SouthKorea’s Retirement Age Reform
affiliations: Pusan National University and Pusan National University

detail.title: Does Extending Working Lives Crowd Out Youth Employment? Evidence from SouthKorea’s Retirement Age Reform
detail.abstract: Population aging across the developed world has prompted many countries to raise statutory retirement ages, yet the labor market consequences of such reforms—particularly for younger cohorts—remain theoretically ambiguous and empirically contested. This paper examines the long-term effects of South Korea's 2016–2017 mandatory retirement age extension to 60, leveraging panel data from the KLIPS (2008–2023) and a quasi-experimental design. Using a Propensity Score Matching Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) framework, we compare wage workers covered by the reform (treatment group) with non-wage workers exempt from retirement mandates (control group). Results indicate that the policy caused a significant decline in youth employment, with effects concentrated in low-wage, labor-intensive industries—sectors characterized by stronger substitutability between older and younger workers and limited job creation. These findings contribute to the economics of ageing literature by providing causal evidence on the intergenerational labor market trade-offs inherent in extending working lives, and underscore the need for complementary policies to mitigate unintended consequences for youth employment.

title: The Managerial Context of ESG Commitment: Economic Conditions and the Duality of Social Capital
affiliations: University of Texas at El Paso - Department of Accounting & Information Systems, University of Texas at El Paso and Louisiana State University Shreveport

detail.title: The Managerial Context of ESG Commitment: Economic Conditions and the Duality of Social Capital
detail.abstract: Drawing on legitimacy theory and behavioral consistency theory, we examine how the socio-economic contexts surrounding managerial decision-making affect firms’ commitments to ESG goals. Our findings reveal nuanced relationships: social capital exerts contrasting effects depending on the economic environment, whereas economic optimism consistently strengthens ESG engagement. Specifically, social capital promotes ESG commitment when there is optimism about the economy but exhibits an adverse side under weaker conditions, dampening managerial willingness to pursue ESG goals. Further analysis shows that these conditional effects are driven primarily by the structural dimension of social capital (networks and associations) rather than by civic norms and values. These results suggest that social networks can serve as catalysts for managerial ESG commitment when their members are confident about their economic welfare but become counterproductive otherwise. The study contributes to understanding how informal local institutions and economic conditions jointly shape managerial ESG behavior.

title: One-Time Windfalls, Lasting Gains: Russia's Maternity Capital and Children's Human-Capital Outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: One-Time Windfalls, Lasting Gains: Russia's Maternity Capital and Children's Human-Capital Outcomes
detail.abstract: Many aging nations attempt to fill cradles with financial incentives, but do such policies also enrich children's lives? We study Russia's Maternity Capital program, a one-time, earmarked family subsidy worth about twice the median annual earned income. Our analysis leverages two policy thresholds built into the program. Among families with at least two children, the benefit is granted to those whose youngest child was born on or after January 1, 2007, and the subsidy can be redeemed only after the child reaches age three. Using regression-discontinuity designs around these cutoffs—birth timing and the redemption-age threshold—and detailed household data, we trace impacts on children's health, nutrition, and education. Children in eligible households grow taller and enjoy better nutrition than their just-ineligible peers; suggestive evidence also points to greater schooling accumulation. When the voucher becomes accessible—at the child's third birthday—households expand children's diets roughly homothetically across calories and macronutrients, with larger increases in lower-income families. This pattern is consistent with tight liquidity constraints and high returns to early-childhood investments. The program thus delivers a demographic baby bonus and a human-capital growth dividend in a single policy.

title: Greening the Grid -Plugging Renewables with Obligations: A Hybrid Neural Network Based Approach
affiliations: Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal and Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal

detail.title: Greening the Grid -Plugging Renewables with Obligations: A Hybrid Neural Network Based Approach
detail.abstract: Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO) mechanism has been notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022 by which a certain percentage of electricity consumption of designated consumers should come from eligible non-fossil sources from April 2024, and non-compliance shall attract a penalty. The mechanism is expected to increase the purchase of electricity from green day-ahead markets (GDAM), which can be a significant step in India's progress towards promotion of renewable energy consumption. Actual market clearing volume in GDAM after RCO has been frequently higher than the volumes predicted using machine learning models, including neural networks and extreme gradient boosting models, indicating the possible effect of a policy shift. The counterfactual simulations forecast higher volumes of green electricity consumption under policy scenario compared to the future no policy scenario, and an increasing trend for the year 2026. When the system is constrained due to stressed market conditions, the policy effects on market clearing volumes weaken. Post-RCO, there has been a fall in green electricity premium, suggesting a tendency towards convergence in electricity prices across conventional and non-conventional market segments during peak hours. Our estimation results applying the before after and control intervention (BACI) framework suggest a significant increase in green electricity consumption compared to electricity consumption in the other market segment, and green electricity becoming relatively less expensive. The findings underscore the significance of mandatory market based green electricity promotion mechanisms in attaining the nation's climate goals.

title: Spark of Change: Has Clean Fuel Policy Ignited Multi-Dimensional Empowerment among Indian Women?
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge, Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal and Indian Institute of Science Education and Research Bhopal

detail.title: Spark of Change: Has Clean Fuel Policy Ignited Multi-Dimensional Empowerment among Indian Women?
detail.abstract: Clean fuel policy enables upward energy mobility that unlock new forms of social and economic agency for women. The study tries to understand how a movement up the energy ladder through a clean fuel policy is socially and economically empowering for women. Using National Family and Health Survey, we explore if rising clean cooking fuel adoption induces multi-dimensional women empowerment among the beneficiaries of Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana (PMUY), 2016. In constructing the empowerment measure, we incorporate dimensions of awareness, economic position, decision-making, and attitude towards domestic violence. Employing difference-indifference , we estimate Intent-To-Treat effects of PMUY on clean fuel adoption, while triple differencing is utilized to estimate scheme impacts on women empowerment among eligible, who uses clean cooking fuel. PMUY has been successful in raising LPG adoption among eligible beneficiaries, which in turn raises economic position, awareness, and decision-making power of women, making them empowered. Following PMUY, we observe that Indian states with higher clean fuel adoption exhibits stronger women empowerment. However, women from Scheduled Caste (SC), and Scheduled Tribe (ST) communities being less likely to use clean fuel, are less likely to be empowered. Clean energy policies have been successful in raising the economic and social position of women in households. However, the underprivileged and marginalized section of society needs special attention with respect to coverage and accessibility, which is expected with Ujjwala 2.0. The study is novel in its approach towards multi-dimensional analysis of women empowerment, and how this is impacted by a clean fuel policy.

title: Comprehensive Literature Review: Private Equity Zombie Firms - Optimal Stopping, Network Contagion, and Phase Transitions in Illiquid Asset Markets
affiliations: Society of Actuaries

detail.title: Comprehensive Literature Review: Private Equity Zombie Firms - Optimal Stopping, Network Contagion, and Phase Transitions in Illiquid Asset Markets
detail.abstract: This literature review synthesizes academic research across seven interconnected domains: zombie firm theory, private equity performance, real options and optimal stopping, network contagion, phase transitions and econophysics, mechanism design, and secondary market liquidity. We identify critical gaps in existing scholarship and establish theoretical foundations for our unified mathematical framework analyzing PE zombie equilibria.

title: Budgeting and Procurement Inefficiencies in Food Provision for Psychiatric Hospitals: A Qualitative Study in Eastern Cape, South Africa
affiliations: University of the Western Cape, University of the Western Cape and South African Medical Research Council

detail.title: Budgeting and Procurement Inefficiencies in Food Provision for Psychiatric Hospitals: A Qualitative Study in Eastern Cape, South Africa
detail.abstract: The study provided strong evidence that limitations in financial management and deficiencies in purchasing practices negatively affect the quality of food provided to adult patients in public psychiatric hospitals. It further reveals structural weaknesses in food service operations within the broader institutional food system. Using the ‘policy triangle’ model developed by Walt & Gilson, the study identifies three key strategies to strengthen food service procurement: flexible budgeting, enhanced supplier accountability, and improved coordination among stakeholders involved in the procurement process. These findings contribute to global debates on nutrition-sensitive interventions by demonstrating how procurement practices can perpetuate health inequalities. The study underscores the need to align institutional food systems with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those addressing hunger, health, and sustainable consumption. As such, institutions need to develop procurement policies that establish and enforce nutritional standards to create more equitable and sustainable food systems in resource-limited healthcare settings.

title: Patent Connections, Business News and Predictable Returns
affiliations: Shenzhen Audencia Financial Technology Institute and Shenzhen Audencia Financial Technology Institute

detail.title: Patent Connections, Business News and Predictable Returns
detail.abstract: We introduce a new framework for return predictability by integrating technological links from patent content with media attention to technology in business news. Using LLMs to measure patent similarity, we first construct a refined peer network. However, we show that traditional patent-linked momentum strategies underperform because they ignore media attention. Enhancing them by weighting patent peers based on their relevance to current technological news generates a significant, robust alpha unexplained by standard factor models or firm characteristics. Our results demonstrate that combining hard technical and soft narrative links offers a superior model for understanding information diffusion and predicting returns.

detail.title: Assessing the Effect of Exchange Rate Fluctuations on Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in Kaduna State

publicationDetails.detailsText: KASU Journal of Economics and Development Studies, Vol 11 Issue 1, No 2 – December 2024

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of exchange Rate fluctuations on small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in Kaduna North Local Government Area, Kaduna State, Nigeria. The study encompasses a population of 1,000 SMEs, from which a sample of 278 businesses was selected using Krejcie and Morgan's formula to ensure a statistically valid representation. The Data were collected through structured questionnaires administered to SME owners, capturing key demographic and business-related information, including exposure to foreign exchange fluctuations which were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods, including a chi-square tests, facilitated by SPSS software, to achieve the outlined objectives. The findings reveal that exchange rate fluctuations significantly affect SME performance, impacting aspects such as sales revenue, credit collection, and supply chain management, and that the development of indigenous small and medium sized businesses in Kaduna North Local government depends largely on exchange rate stability. The results suggest the need for more robust foreign exchange management strategies and supportive policies to mitigate the adverse effects of exchange rate fluctuations on SMEs.

detail.abstract: This study aims to examine the impact of cloud-based data storage and internet accessibility on supporting decision-making in financial service institutions regulated by the Saudi Central Bank. The study addresses the challenges faced by these institutions when adopting cloud computing, particularly in relation to regulatory compliance, data governance, information security, and cybersecurity requirements. A design-oriented research methodology supported by a simulated case study was adopted to develop an integrated model that links cloud-based data storage, internet accessibility, and governance and regulatory controls. The study analyzes the impact of this model on decision-making at operational, financial, and strategic levels. The findings indicate that adopting cloud computing within a robust data governance framework and strong information security and cybersecurity controls significantly enhances the speed of data access and the quality of information used for decision-making, while maintaining compliance with regulatory requirements set by the Saudi Central Bank. The study concludes that the effective use of cloud computing in financial institutions depends not only on technological capabilities but also on the integration of governance, security, and regulatory considerations to support efficient and sustainable decision-making.

title: Environmental-Unfriendly Tax Avoidance
affiliations: Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, University of Navarra, IESE Business School and

detail.title: Environmental-Unfriendly Tax Avoidance
detail.abstract: This paper examines how firms use carbon allowances to reduce corporate tax burdens by routing allowance transactions through internal trading hubs in low-tax jurisdictions and by exploiting fluctuations in carbon prices. Using a dataset that captures the universe of carbonallowance transactions in the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) from 2014 to 2020, we document that roughly 35% of corporate groups operate internal hubs that collect and redistribute allowances across affiliated entities required to surrender them. Many of these hubs are located in jurisdictions with low statutory tax rates or in recognized tax havens, resulting in significantly lower effective tax rates for hubs relative to other entities within the same multinational group. With such internal reallocations of allowances, firms can generate substantial tax savings. We further document that such tax-motivated internal trading and profit shifting is associated with lower investment in decarbonization and higher volumes of allowance surrenders. Taken together, it appears that tax avoidance alleviates the financial pressure to reduce emissions.

title: When Machines Persuade Better Than Humans: Generative AI, Cognitive Constraints, and Promotional Effectiveness
affiliations: University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business, University of Maryland - Robert H. Smith School of Business,  and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: When Machines Persuade Better Than Humans: Generative AI, Cognitive Constraints, and Promotional Effectiveness

publicationDetails.detailsText: Boston University Questrom School of Business Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Boston University Questrom School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into commercial platforms offers unprecedented opportunities for scalable, personalized promotional communication. This study examines the effects of GenAI-based production promotion on customer purchase decisions in the context of online product promotion. Partnering with a chain restaurant, we conducted a randomized field experiment in which customers were assigned to receive one of four types of messages: AI-generated personalized messages, AI-generated generic messages, human-generated generic messages, or coupons only. Results show that both AI-generated message types significantly enhance customer purchasing behavior compared with human-generated ones, with AI-generated personalized messages increasing daily order amounts by 14.3% and AI-generated generic messages by 10.4%. Moderation analyses reveal that AI-generic messages are particularly effective in high cognitive load contexts (e.g., in the workplace or during working hours), while AI-generated personalized messages maintain effectiveness across all contexts. We employ the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM) to identify a two-tier cognitive mechanism underlying these findings. First, AI-generated messages are more readable than human-generated messages, reducing comprehension barriers for persuasion. Second, we find that AI-generated generic messages leverage strong peripheral persuasion cues. In contrast, AI-generated personalized messages incorporate both peripheral and central route elements, enabling dual-pathway persuasion. This research contributes to the Information Systems (IS) literature by providing causal field evidence on the promotional effectiveness of generative AI, advancing cognitive load and ELM theories in the context of AI-generated content, and offering practical insights for AI-driven customer engagement strategies.

title: The hidden Zimbabwean Blockchain Technology Engine: A permanent solution to poverty and inequality in Africa.
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: The hidden Zimbabwean Blockchain Technology Engine: A permanent solution to poverty and inequality in Africa.
detail.abstract: The Blockchain Technology (BT) wave is currently moving across the African continent. Nigeria recently launched a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), Mauritius regulated Crypto Assets (CAs), and South Africa is working on Proof Of Concepts (POC) on the use of CBDC for both wholesale and retail purposes. Having banned financial institutions from facilitating CAs transactions, the Zimbabwean government is now reconsidering the regulation of CAs. The issue of crypto regulation in Africa is the main cause why the continent is lagging in the adoption of blockchain applications. Another challenge is that of blockchain infrastructure and skills, which are lacking in the continent. Hence, the objective of this study is to identify Zimbabwean Financial Technology (FinTech) companies and their contributions towards the adoption of BT in Africa, particularly in finance. To achieve the above objective, a non-empirical, exploratory research was conducted in the form of an online desktop review. It was found that Zimbabwe has the following FinTech companies: Mirracle Consultants, Coinmadi, Uhuru Wallet, BillMari, ZIMBOCASH, Capital Factor, and FlexFinTx; which have a combined effect of improving the African socio-economic conditions.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes a system-based framework for sustainable YouTube channel growth, focusing on the interaction between search visibility, audience retention, monetization mechanisms, and algorithmic risk signals.

Rather than treating growth as a collection of isolated optimization tactics, the study conceptualizes YouTube channels as dynamic systems shaped by platform governance, automated enforcement mechanisms, and long-term behavioral signals.

The framework outlines how content strategy, traffic composition, and audience–content alignment interact to produce scalable yet resilient growth models, particularly in an environment where algorithmic risk assessment increasingly influences visibility and channel continuity.

title: Validating GenAI Work: Expert Quality Assurance in Contract Analysis
affiliations: UC Davis, Graduate School of Management and UC Davis

detail.title: Validating GenAI Work: Expert Quality Assurance in Contract Analysis
detail.abstract: We demonstrate quality assurance protocols for GenAI-assisted extraction of accounting measurement details from contracts, addressing the governance gap in professional services. Analyzing 1,772 debt covenants for off-balance-sheet lease restrictions, we compare manual coding (three months, $8,000) with GenAI processing (one week, $1,300). Applying Bhargava and Kishore's (2025) framework, we establish that high-stakes contract analysis demands rigorous ex-ante prompt development rather than ex-post verification alone. For academics, we show how GenAI's semantic interpretation expands construct validity beyond keyword searches while requiring explicit construct scope decisions. For practitioners, we provide protocols that reallocate expert effort from routine coding to developing domain-specific prompts, validating semantic boundaries, and diagnosing systematic errors. These validation protocols apply across professional services requiring complex document interpretation, from financial reporting and tax compliance to credit assessment and litigation e-discovery.

detail.abstract: Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) have emerged as a foundational technology for monitoring, data acquisition, and intelligent decision-making across diverse domains such as environmental monitoring, healthcare, industrial automation, and smart infrastructure. A WSN consists of a large number of resourceconstrained sensor nodes capable of sensing, processing, and wirelessly transmitting data to centralized or distributed sinks. Despite extensive research over the past two decades, real-world deployments of WSNs continue to face critical challenges related to energy efficiency, scalability, reliability, security, and environmental adaptability. This paper presents a comprehensive and structured analysis of Wireless Sensor Networks, covering their architectural design, classification, deployment environments, communication models, and application domains. Furthermore, it critically examines the key technical challenges and limitations that hinder large-scale adoption and reliability outside laboratory conditions.

title: The Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth: A Playbook for Societal Impact at Scale
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business, Independent, Independent and Independent

detail.title: The Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth: A Playbook for Societal Impact at Scale
detail.abstract:
The Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth (the Center) was launched in 2013 to advance equitable and sustainable economic growth by accelerating financial inclusion worldwide. The Center seeks to move beyond traditional corporate philanthropy by pairing philanthropic capital with Mastercard's core business assets (data, technology, expertise, and networks) to create a scalable “doing well by doing good” model. By 2024, the Center had helped bring nearly a billion people into the formal financial system, and the Center was preparing for the next shift—from a digital economy to a data- and AI-driven economy—while keeping its focus on outcomes such as long-term financial health. This case presents the Center's playbook for impact at scale, including an organizational framework built around Insights, Impact, and Influence and a program development approach of Test, Iterate, and Scale to build evidence-based solutions with partners. Examples of the Center's global work illustrate how multi-sector partnerships, measurement, iteration, and replication help convert insights into scalable programs. The case closes by asking how the Center should adapt its model, partnerships, and priorities as new technologies and contexts reshape the inclusive growth agenda.

Excerpt

The Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth:A Playbook for Societal Impact at Scale

Remember this rule of thumb: if you want to go wide, go with government. If you want to go deep, go with NGOs and academic institutions. If you want to go fast, go with the private sector. And if you want to go far, you must go together.

—Shamina Singh, Founder and President, Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth

As modern digital finance tools like mobile money and online banking became much more common over the 2010s and 2020s, millions of people transitioned to the digital economy with varying degrees of success. Together with its partners, the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth (the Center), Mastercard's social impact hub, focused on easing that transition with its mission to advance equitable and sustainable economic growth and financial inclusion around the world. This focus was integral to Mastercard's commitment to bring 1 billion people and 50 million small businesses into the formal financial system by 2025. As of 2024, the company had reached 960 million individuals and already surpassed its small business goal with a total of 65 million micro and small businesses connected. This progress aligned with broader global trends, including the World Bank's 2025 Global Findex report, which found that 79% of adults globally had a financial account, with digital payments driving much of this growth. As the shift to digital continued, the transition to a data- and AI-driven economy was projected to accelerate, and the Center positioned itself to continue to adapt its strategy to meet these evolving trends.

title: Investment Mobilisation as Infrastructure A Governance Architecture for Converting Capital Availability into Capital Deployment

detail.title: Investment Mobilisation as Infrastructure A Governance Architecture for Converting Capital Availability into Capital Deployment

detail.abstract:
Despite unprecedented global liquidity, capital deployment into productive and developmentally meaningful investments remains persistently constrained. This paper argues that the capital deployment gap is not primarily a function of capital scarcity, deal origination, or risk pricing, but of missing mobilisation infrastructure. In practice, investment opportunities frequently fail upstream due to weak readiness articulation, unclear decision accountability, fragmented preparation standards, and insufficient governance assurance.

The paper advances a conceptual and institutional thesis that investment mobilisation should be treated as infrastructure rather than episodic advisory activity or ad hoc project preparation. It introduces the Investment Mobilisation Management System (IMMS) as a neutral, governance-oriented architecture that standardises readiness signalling, preparation discipline, decision governance, integrity, and pipeline stewardship across institutions and jurisdictions. By reducing transaction costs, improving comparability, and enhancing decision legitimacy, mobilisation infrastructure can materially improve the probability of capital deployment without distorting allocation decisions.

This paper advances a conceptual and institutional thesis. It does not specify implementation methodologies, diagnostic criteria, or operational procedures. Such elements are intentionally excluded, as mobilisation infrastructure depends on contextual governance, institutional capacity, and stewarded adoption rather than universal process prescription.

title: Discrimination as an Agency Problem: Multi-dimensional Screening and Optimal Contracts

detail.title: Discrimination as an Agency Problem: Multi-dimensional Screening and Optimal Contracts
detail.abstract: The paper proposes and analyses a screening model to study discriminatory decisions resulted from an agency problem in hierarchical organizations. An agent who is in charge of promotion decisions (e.g. management of a firm) may or may not have a discriminatory taste toward candidates, while a principal (e.g. the owner of a firm) is unbiased, only cares about her profit, and does not observe each candidate’s quality. The agent’s private information structure shows distinct features as a real multi-dimensional screening problem--no information aggregation: a three-dimensional screening problem analyzed here (incomplete information on the agent's discrimination type and quality levels of the two candidates) cannot be simplified to a lower-dimensional problem. That is, summary information is insufficient because each of the reports in a direct mechanism setting plays a unique role in the principal's understanding of the given screening problem and derivation of an optimal contract.

title: Territorial Partitions and Collective Identity: A Comparative Study of Azerbaijan and Ireland

detail.title: Territorial Partitions and Collective Identity: A Comparative Study of Azerbaijan and Ireland
detail.abstract: Azerbaijan and Ireland share a notable historical similarity: each was once a relatively unified society later divided through external intervention. Despite enduring linguistic, cultural, and historical continuities, political partition exposed each to distinct state systems, producing long-term divergence in development and identity articulation. This paper adopts a comparative, institution-centered perspective, conceptualizing identity change as a cumulative outcome of prolonged exposure to contrasting state projects and patterns of recognition. By comparing the Azerbaijani and Irish cases, the study shows how similar starting conditions can yield divergent identity outcomes depending on institutional depth and historical sequencing.

title: Optimal Mechanism Design with Post-Allocation Signal
affiliations: , University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Fuqua School of Business and University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Mechanism Design with Post-Allocation Signal
detail.abstract: We study the design of the optimal mechanism in a setting with one buyer and one item in which the seller receives a binary signal correlated with the buyer's type after the allocation decision and can condition the payment on the signal realization. The optimal mechanism depends on the correlation between the signal and the buyer's type through the conditional probability of the signal given the type, which we call the buyer's belief function. Under the standard monotone likelihood ratio property (MLRP), we establish that the curvature of the buyer's belief function plays a central role. Full surplus extraction is achievable if and only if the belief function is convex in the buyer's type. In contrast, when beliefs are concave, the optimal allocation takes a non-monotonic form: the item is fully allocated to types outside an intermediate range, and not allocated otherwise. We further establish that, in the case of concave beliefs, the optimal mechanism can be implemented as a state-contingent posted payment offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis. We provide a structural characterization of the optimal deterministic mechanism under general belief functions: the type space is partitioned into several regions, depending on the curvature of the belief function, and in each region, we either have full surplus extraction or a state-contingent posted payment. Finally, we show how our results can be extended to a setting with multiple buyers.

title: Assessment of Constraints in Use of Non-motorized Transport in Lahore

detail.title: Assessment of Constraints in Use of Non-motorized Transport in Lahore
detail.abstract: A balanced infrastructure for both motorized and non-motorized transportation is one of the challenges for urban mobility in Lahore. With minimal consideration for non-motorized transport, most of Lahore's road infrastructure has been designed for motorized transportation. Urban road networks are under stress due to the unrelenting plying of motor vehicles, which causes congestion for most of the day. The research explores existing barriers and difficulties that impact the utilization of non-motorized transport for sustainable urban mobility. Reliability analysis was applied to validate the response of households and experts. Regression Analysis was used to identify paramount constraints for the smooth operation of non-motorized transport. The paper recommends policy measures for rationalization and smooth operation of non-motorized transport in Lahore. ☆ This article is part of a special issue entitled: 'Green public transport' published in Case Studies on Transport Policy.

title: Bridging Nature and Urbanity Through Green Roof Resilience Framework (GRF): A Thematic Review

detail.title: Bridging Nature and Urbanity Through Green Roof Resilience Framework (GRF): A Thematic Review
detail.abstract: The impacts of climate change pose a critical research challenge for sustainability. Despite growing awareness of green roofs as nature-based solutions, a significant gap exists in understanding their role in urban resilience. The research reviews thematic perspectives of green roofs in improving urban resilience. The paper used the PRISMA framework to systematically review the literature on green roofs and climate change, utilizing the keywords "green roof*" and climate change" in the Web of Science database. Bibliometric and thematic analysis is used to observe research trends from 123 publications that meet inclusion criteria, which include selected keywords, language, and publication type. Recurrent themes included urban heat islands, stormwater runoff, thermal comfort, biodiversity conservation, carbon footprint reduction, urban agriculture, and human well-being. The study proposes the Green Roof Resilience Framework (GRF), which combines these ideas into a systematic method for enhancing urban resilience. The research advocates for mainstreaming green roofs into adaptation planning, envisioning the creation of sustainable and resilient societies.

title: When Does Schedule Consistency Improve Shift Worker Productivity?
affiliations: Arizona State University (ASU) - Supply Chain Management, , Donbei University of Finance and Economics and Dongbei University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: When Does Schedule Consistency Improve Shift Worker Productivity?

declarations.funderStatement: This study is supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72172027, 72293563, 72232001).

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management (M&SOM). Authors contributed equally to this work.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: Shift workers make up a significant portion of the labor force in major countries and are widespread across industries. Their work schedules often involve odd hours and inconsistencies over time, deviating from regular day workers. Lu et al. (2022) introduced a two-dimensional measure for shift worker schedule consistency, namely, the hour-of-the-day and the day-of-the-week consistencies, and demonstrated their efficacy in improving labor productivity for grocery store cashiers. We expand this nascent literature in several ways. Methodology/results: Using data collected from warehouse workers performing picking and loading tasks, our context is differentiated by the inclusion of night hours and a piece-rate pay structure. The former enables us to show that hour-of-the-day consistency improves productivity only during day hours; it is in fact detrimental to productivity, at an even larger magnitude, during sleep hours. We revise the rhythm-synchronizing theory proposed by Lu et al. (2022) to accommodate this heterogeneity. The latter affords a comparison of effect sizes across the two most common pay structures for shift workers. We demonstrate that hour-of-the-day and day-of-the-week consistencies’ impact on productivity are four- and eight-times larger under piece-rate pay than under hourly pay. We further consider how two environmental factors, inclement weather and extreme temperature—both easily accessible via weather forecasts by schedulers, attenuate hour-of-the-day consistency’s effect. Managerial implications: Departing from existing perspective that both schedule consistency dimensions are effective, we show robust evidence that day-of-the-week consistency not only has a larger impact, improving productivity by 9.20% for a 1st-to-3rd quartile change compared with hour-of-the-day consistency’s 2.03%, but is also relatively stable across days and resistant to moderation by environmental factors. Thus, it should be the primary operational lever for schedulers, especially given its relative ease of use in practice. We also find schedule consistency to be most beneficial for new hires, with its impact waning as workers accumulate experience. The speed of this attenuation is, however, much slower than previously reported. We illustrate how these insights can be easily incorporated into a consistency-aware scheduling policy through numerical studies.

title: Neighborhood Matters: Examining Socio-Demographic and Spatial Disparities in Active School Travel in the United States
affiliations: , University of Texas at Arlington, University of Texas at Arlington and

detail.title: Neighborhood Matters: Examining Socio-Demographic and Spatial Disparities in Active School Travel in the United States
detail.abstract: Active School Travel (AST) offers children vital opportunities for physical activity, independence, and neighborhood engagement. However, AST rate in the United States continue to decline and remains unevenly distributed across communities. This study examines socio-demographic and spatial disparities in AST using data from the 2022 National Household Travel Survey (NHTS), the first post-pandemic national-level travel dataset. We analyze school travel behavior among 2,190 children aged 5-17 using descriptive statistics, bivariate comparisons, and binary logistic regression models based on usual and survey-day travel modes. Findings reveal that only 11.9% of children walk or bike to school, with AST strongly influenced by age, school distance, urban form, and car access. Distance emerged as the strongest predictor, with the likelihood of AST declining sharply beyond one mile and becoming extremely rare for children living more than two miles from school. Children living in denser, renterdominant urban neighborhoods have significantly higher odds of using active modes, whereas those in suburban and rural communities exhibit much lower rates. Socioeconomic disparities indicate that, for transportation-disadvantaged families, AST may function more as necessity than choice. This study provides one of the earliest assessments of school travel behavior in a post-pandemic landscape and identifies key determinants of AST. Our findings stress the importance of integrating land use planning, school siting decisions, and neighborhood design strategies to create child-friendly environments that support AST. This research offers timely insights for planners, policymakers, and school officials seeking to promote active, healthy, and inclusive mobility for children.

title: The Silent Collapse: Quantifying the Equity-Feasibility Gap in Green Humanitarian Logistics Who Suffers First When Networks Degrade?

detail.title: The Silent Collapse: Quantifying the Equity-Feasibility Gap in Green Humanitarian Logistics Who Suffers First When Networks Degrade?
detail.abstract: Highlights • Introduces the equity frontier-the stress threshold where service inequality exceeds humanitarian bounds while networks remain feasible • Reveals structural baseline inequity: 2 of 12 baseline-feasible networks (16.7%) violate equity thresholds even at zero stress • Across 760 stress scenarios (300 demand, 220 capacity, 240 time), 25.4% of feasible solutions (85 of 335) violate equity thresholds • Quantifies geographic disadvantage: 100% of solutions with peripheral data (N=156) have PP > 1 (mean PP=2.54; max=6.86), with peripheral populations waiting 2-7× longer • Under demand stress specifically, reveals Complexity Trap: medium-scale networks exhibit highest violation rate (58.3% vs. 21.8% small, 46.2% large) • Finds inequitable scenarios impose 1.71× higher mean deprivation costs (2.08× higher total deprivation costs), quantifying the human cost of "Silent Collapse" • Demonstrates equity frontier precedes feasibility frontier by median ~65 percentage points under demand stress (range 30-110).

detail.abstract: Highlights • Proposes a Time-Adaptive Framework operationalizing Van Wassenhove's (2006) agility-leanness dichotomy for computational solver selection • Introduces the Handover Protocol-a formal mechanism for GA→ICA transition at phase boundaries with archive-based seeding • Validates GA as the rapid-response engine: 36% faster on 400 runs (1.22s vs. 1.91s; p < 0.001) with 38% lower solve-time dispersion (σ). • Shows phase-dependent trade-offs: GA is faster and more reliable in early response, while ICA is suited for longer planning horizons where additional compute is acceptable. • Provides Taguchi-based parameter screening (GA L9 orthogonal; ICA L18 nearorthogonal) with ANOVA-style factor contributions and recommended settings for reproducible deployment. • Uses checkpoint tracking (objective and diversity trajectories) to operationalize a handover trigger from rapid-response to planning optimization.

title: Transformer Architectures for Human Emotion Understanding in Voice Interfaces
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Transformer Architectures for Human Emotion Understanding in Voice Interfaces
detail.abstract: This study examines recent advances in speech-based emotion understanding for voice interfaces, with a particular focus on transformer architectures and their role in improving affective intelligence. The paper synthesizes state-of-the-art transformer-based, hybrid, and multimodal approaches to speech emotion recognition, emphasizing their performance in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and real-world deployability within intelligent voice systems (Onyekwelu-Udoka et al. 2025; Portal et al. 2025). By reviewing comparative empirical evidence, the study highlights how transformer models-often integrated with convolutional or recurrent components-consistently outperform traditional CNN and LSTM-based architectures, especially under cross-corpus evaluation and low-resource training conditions (Alroobaea 2024; Akinpelu et al. 2024). These models demonstrate superior contextual modeling, robustness to speaker variability, and improved generalization across domains. The findings further indicate that hybrid and multimodal transformer frameworks enhance emotion recognition by effectively fusing acoustic, linguistic, and contextual cues without imposing prohibitive computational costs. The paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of these advances for the development of empathetic voice interfaces, assistive technologies, and human-robot interaction systems, where reliable and context-aware emotional understanding is critical for natural and socially adaptive communication (Mishra et al. 2025; Duan et al. 2024).

title: Superintelligence and Law
affiliations: Hebrew University of Jerusalem

detail.title: Superintelligence and Law
detail.abstract: The prospect of artificial superintelligence—AI agents that can generally outperform humans in cognitive tasks and economically valuable activities—will transform the legal order as we know it. Operating autonomously or under only limited human oversight, AI agents will assume a growing range of roles in the legal system. First, in making consequential decisions and taking real-world actions, AI agents will become de facto subjects of law. Second, to cooperate and compete with other actors (human or non-human), AI agents will harness conventional legal instruments and institutions such as contracts and courts, becoming consumers of law. Third, to the extent AI agents perform the functions of writing, interpreting, and administering law, they will become producers and enforcers of law. These developments, whenever they ultimately occur, will call into question fundamental assumptions in legal theory and doctrine, especially to the extent they ground the legitimacy of legal institutions in their human origins. Attempts to align AI agents with extant human law will also face new challenges as AI agents will not only be a primary target of law, but a core user of law and contributor to law. To contend with the advent of superintelligence, lawmakers—new and old—will need to be clear-eyed, recognizing both the opportunity to shape legal institutions as society braces for superintelligence and the reality that, in the longer run, this may be a joint human-AI endeavor.

detail.abstract: The effectiveness of security operations often depends on cooperation between national armies. Such cooperation can be particularly important when international borders are porous and armed groups can operate across borders. We investigate how the creation of an international armed force that could operate across international borders (the G5-Sahel Joint Force) together with improved communication between national armies affected conflict dynamics in the Sahel region. Relying on a regression discontinuity design, we find that the G5 mission lowered the intensity of conflict locally in its zone of operation, especially along border segments more porous due to their geographical features or ethnic composition. Further analysis of geographical conflict propagation patterns indicates that the G5-Sahel force facilitated security operations in border areas.

title: Trumpism And The Substantial End Of The Us-Eu Alliance
affiliations: Università degli Studi Guglielmo Marconi

detail.title: Trumpism And The Substantial End Of The Us-Eu Alliance
detail.abstract: This article examines the geopolitical, constitutional, and strategic implications of Trumpism for the transatlantic relationship, suggesting that recent shifts in United States foreign and domestic policy may contribute to a significant reconfiguration of longstanding patterns of cooperation between America and Europe. Building upon an earlier monographic analysis of the ideological and institutional trajectories of liberal democracies, the study situates the phenomenon within a broader framework that includes renewed currents of political and economic nationalism and a more selective approach to international engagement. Developments affecting constitutional checks and balances, together with an increasingly decision-centred conception of sovereignty, are considered as potentially indicative of meaningful changes in the functioning of American liberal democracy. Against this background, the article analyses the turn towards economic protectionism, the expanded use of tariffs as a policy instrument, and a more openly critical posture towards the European Union. Particular attention is devoted to the new National Security Strategy, including its references to the Monroe Doctrine and related interpretive extensions, which may signal a recalibration of unilateral and multilateral commitments and a reshaping of alliance priorities.

title: The Sixth Layer: The Legal Infrastructure for Physical Artificial Intelligence in China
affiliations: University of Southern California Gould School of Law

detail.title: The Sixth Layer: The Legal Infrastructure for Physical Artificial Intelligence in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
This Article offers the first comprehensive study of how law serves as critical infrastructure supporting China’s development of physical artificial intelligence (AI)—AI systems embedded in and operating through the physical world. Drawing on an in-depth analysis of Chinese legislation and enforcement practices governing autonomous driving, robotics, drones, and brain–computer interfaces, this Article argues that Chinese law functions as the sixth layer of the AI ecosystem, alongside energy, compute, cloud, foundation models, and applications.

Unlike generative AI, physical AI systems often require testing in public environments, and the acquisition of high-quality training data is more costly and time-consuming. To overcome these challenges, Chinese law has been deliberately engineered to perform three interlocking functions. First, law stimulates adoption through top-level policy design and regulatory sandboxes that authorize large-scale regional experimentation. Wider deployment reduces unit costs and accelerates adoption, while simultaneously generating operational data that enhances model performance and system reliability. Second, law enables unification at scale by imposing technical standards that discipline product design and production. Crucially, these rules also standardize data collection and facilitate the construction of large-scale data platforms. Third, law fortifies China’s competitive moat by restricting the collection of important data and the cross-border transfer of data generated through deployment itself.

Taken together, these legal functions—stimulation, unification, and fortification—creates a  unique, state-engineered data flywheel by transforming real-world deployment into a durable source of data advantage.  This early deployment-based experience and domestic standard-setting also enhances China’s influence within international standard-setting bodies and further expands exports of Chinese AI products overseas. As China approaches the technological frontier, it has begun to impose more stringent legal requirements on its products, thereby positioning itself as an increasingly influential rule-setter in global AI governance.

China’s law-as-infrastructure approach carries profound domestic and global implications. By prioritizing rapid deployment and large-scale data capture, it risks weakening labor and safety protections while exacerbating chronic industrial overcapacity. As domestic pressures mount, outward expansion represents the primary pathway through which China can externalize some of the economic and social costs generated by rapid AI-driven transformation at home.

At the same time, notwithstanding escalating geopolitical tensions, China’s advances in physical AI may create incentives for American firms to engage in selective cooperation with their Chinese counterparts. However, the U.S. government has found it difficult to emulate China’s model of state-led coordination, given the institutional constraints it faces. Instead, it relies heavily on Big Tech firms, which increasingly constitute the backbone of U.S. competitiveness in physical AI. The United States must therefore strike a delicate balance in determining the extent to which it is willing to tolerate concentrated private power as a substitute for state coordination in the global race for leadership in AI.  Above all, the centrality of cost in China’s data flywheel underscores the imperative for the United States to strengthen its industrial capacity. Rebuilding domestic manufacturing is not merely about winning the AI race—it is an urgent matter of national security.

title: Learning to Prompt: Human Adaptation in Production with Generative AI
affiliations: University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

detail.title: Learning to Prompt: Human Adaptation in Production with Generative AI
detail.abstract: What is the role of human input in AI-assisted production? Humans interact with generative AI through combinations of words called prompts. A key feature of human input is adaptation: users dynamically modify their prompts based on their understanding of AI. I empirically investigate two types of adaptation: (1) adaptation to new AI versions, referring to how people change their prompts in response to AI upgrades; (2) adaptation to outputs from previous prompts, referring to how people adjust their prompts iteratively to converge on desired outcomes. I study this adaptation using prompt-level data from Midjourney, a leading AI image generator. First, users adapt to AI upgrades by writing different words in their prompts. By submitting prompts written for the old version to the new AI and vice versa, I decompose the output shifts as arising from prompt changes (73%), AI changes (20%), and a residual (7%), implying complementarity between AI and human inputs. Second, prompts evolve within the creative process of an artwork. I estimate a structural model of the creative process using the sequential search framework. Counterfactual shows that without human adaptation, users need three times more prompts to achieve data-observed results. Both results highlight the importance of human judgment and adaptation in the creative process.

detail.abstract: Does the 2026 United States intervention in Venezuela mark the death of the non-intervention norm in International Relations? Drawing on practice theory and contemporary social norms scholarship, we argue that the episode is analytically significant not because it violated non-intervention, but because it abandoned the performative practices associated with the norm, through which such violations have historically been rendered intelligible and contestable. We develop a framework that distinguishes between norm performativity and institutional robustness, generating four ideal types of norms: embedded, ritualised, residual, and defunct. Applying this framework, we show that while non-intervention remains institutionally robust, Washington’s neglect of the usual vocabulary and diplomatic practices surrounding the intervention marks a shift in its position from embedded to residual engagement with the norm. We conclude by discussing the implications of this change for both social norms theory and the practice of non-intervention as one of the key pillars of the contemporary global order.

Primary data were collected through a structure questionnaire from 200 respondents in Dangote Flour Mills Plc, Illorin. Four research hypotheses were examined and result showed that there is a significant relationship between work environment and Employees' self esteem at 0.05 limits [r(198) = 0.541, p<0.01]. title: Dual-Sourcing in an Assembly System: A Simple and Effective Critical-Set Base-Surge Policy
affiliations: Soochow University, , Duke University - Fuqua School of Business and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Information Management and Engineering

detail.title: Dual-Sourcing in an Assembly System: A Simple and Effective Critical-Set Base-Surge Policy
detail.abstract: To enhance supply chain resilience, assembly manufacturers increasingly adopt dual-sourcing strategies, utilizing both regular and faster but costlier express sources for each key component. While research has focused on single-item systems, coordinating dual-sourced orders across multiple components in an assembly system remains under-explored. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Critical-Set Base-Surge (CSBS) policy, which combines a constant order policy for regular sources to meet base demand with a Critical-Set (CS) policy for express sources to handle surge demand. Under the CS policy, only components within a "critical set" are replenished from the express sources, raising their net inventory levels to a common threshold. By uncovering a weaker form of additive separability and demonstrating the exponential convergence of states under the CSBS policy, we establish a theoretical bound on its performance and demonstrate its asymptotic optimality as regular lead times increase. The results can be extended to settings where only a subset of components are dual-sourced. Numerical experiments show that, compared to benchmark policies that apply the Tailored Base-Surge policy, the CSBS policy achieves substantial optimality gap reductions. Furthermore, we propose a CSBS policy with easy-to-compute parameters and demonstrate that it delivers performance comparable with the CSBS policy.

title: Stop Making Sense: Reviving the Robinson-Patman Act and the Economics of Intermediate Price Discrimination
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School and George Mason University, Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Stop Making Sense: Reviving the Robinson-Patman Act and the Economics of Intermediate Price Discrimination

publicationDetails.detailsText: George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-03
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We examine the modern theoretical and economic literature analyzing intermediate good price discrimination, and its bearing on recent attempts to revive enforcement of the Robinson-Patman Act. While economists have replaced economically incoherent arguments with internally consistent theoretical models that show that it is possible for intermediate good price discrimination to decrease welfare, the literature has been much less successful in providing theoretical guidance or empirical evidence on whether and when these possibility theorems apply to potential real-world cases outside of the academic blackboard. When models instead incorporate key institutional features of pricing that large firms actually use, such as non-linear pricing and bargaining, economic analyses find that restricting intermediate good price discrimination increases input prices and reduces welfare.  

The lack of useful guidance from models and empirical evidence suggesting potential harm is particularly relevant when one considers the history and content of Robinson-Patman. Like the economic literature, neither the statute nor its history at the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) provides useful guidance for enforcing the statute consistent with modern antitrust principles. The statute's protectionist origins (although not necessarily it's actual language) and the FTC’s misguided application show instead that enforcement had little purpose other than to try to constrain innovation in manufacturing and retailing by large, efficient firms. The companion piece to this paper, Zombie Antitrust: Is Robinson Patman a Dead Law Walking? details the Act’s history, including the reasons for disuse after decades of aggressive FTC enforcement and the recent efforts at revival. While cases “targeted” towards harmful discriminatory input pricing sound useful in theory, such a strategy appears impractical. Moreover, for any harms from discriminatory prices identified by the modern economic literature, the antitrust law already can apply a nuanced policy that considers both the benefits and costs of challenged practices under existing Sherman and Clayton Act precedent. Thus, there is little marginal benefit from reviving the Act, a statute ill-suited to such a task.

detail.abstract:
Most approaches to AI safety focus on optimizing performance within a predefined Decision Space. Yet empirical failures in autonomous and generative systems increasingly reveal a deeper problem: systems can operate correctly while interpreting reality incorrectly. This paper introduces Semantic Physics as a causal framework for analyzing and stabilizing the relationship between an agent’s internal Meaning Space and the physical world.

We argue that autonomy requires not only functional reliability but ontological coherence. Building on semiotics, decision theory, complexity science, and structural causal models, the paper proposes the concept of Semantic Structural Causal Semantics (SSCS), in which meaning acts as a causal bottleneck between perception and decision. To operationalize this framework, we introduce the Semantic Stability Index (SSI), a composite metric designed to detect semantic divergence, normative incoherence, and contextual fragility in real time.

Using the Penrose Triangle as a diagnostic probe, the paper demonstrates how generative systems exhibit local consistency while failing at global ontological coherence—a phenomenon termed the Penrose Moment. Backward Target Analysis (BTA) is presented as an inverse causal operator that reconstructs latent meaning structures from observable decisions, enabling the identification of semantic failure points before they manifest as physical or organizational risks.

By formalizing meaning as a measurable and governable dimension of autonomous systems, Semantic Physics extends existing AI safety paradigms beyond statistical reliability toward epistemic and ontological robustness. The framework provides a foundation for certifiable autonomous interpretation and offers a new perspective on governance, responsibility, and risk in AI-driven decision architectures.

detail.abstract:
Corporate America is increasingly shaping our everyday lives. But Corporate America is not merely an abstract concept. It is the aggregate of thousands of corporations, each operating independently and guided by its own set of policies. From political donations to diversity, corporations—and the governance policies that drive them—wield the power to transform society. But how do corporations adopt their policies? A rich literature has highlighted several channels through which governance
practices disseminate across corporate America. This Article is the first to identify an important and previously overlooked channel: peer corporations.

Over the last fifteen years, corporations have increasingly identified other corporations as their peers. These designations were mostly spurred in response to investors’ concerns regarding executive compensation and to benchmark executive pay against a group of peers. But as this article demonstrates, peer groups do more than that—they help corporations identify policies and practices to emulate in a variety of areas, ranging from governance to diversity to environmental protection. This Article terms this tendency as “peer group governance.” Despite the growing use of peer groups and the impact it has on corporate actions, scholars have not explored how corporations select their peers and use them over time. This Article sheds new light on the use of peer groups among public corporations. In doing so, the Article makes three key contributions to literature. First, using a first of its kind, hand-collected dataset of all peer group designations amongst the S&P 1500 companies from 2005 to 2021, it offers the first detailed empirical account of both the growing use, attributes, and composition of peer groups. Second, using data on the governance attributes of each corporation in the S&P 1500, and interviews with directors and general counsels of public corporation, the Article identifies peer groups as an important channel for the transfer of corporate governance policies and practices. Third, the article delineates the wide-ranging implications of peer group governance on SEC disclosure rules, investor policies and shareholder advocacy efforts.

title: The Option Value of Flexibility: Auto-Ship versus On-Demand Competition under Input Price Shock
affiliations: ,  and Southeast University

detail.title: The Option Value of Flexibility: Auto-Ship versus On-Demand Competition under Input Price Shock
detail.abstract: The retail playbook is being rewritten by the convergence of two distinct philosophies: auto-ship, which puts purchasing on "autopilot" to lock consumers in, and on-demand, which preserves the freedom to switch and shop around. As firms increasingly adopt both formats, a fundamental question emerges: when does a dual-mode menu profitably segment the market, and when does it backfire through cannibalization and intensified rivalry? We address this by modeling a duopoly where firms endogenously choose a mode-autoship, on-demand, or dual-mode-under input price shocks and two-dimensional consumer heterogeneity (horizontal fit and search frictions). Our analysis reveals that input price uncertainty is the primary determinant of equilibrium strategy. The dual mode is not universally superior; it creates value only under moderate input price uncertainty by successfully segmenting "convenience seekers" from "bargain hunters". We derive two counterintuitive insights that challenge the conventional view of lock-in. First, search frictions and input price uncertainty act as substitutes: while high search costs typically favor lock-in, high uncertainty generates a substantial "option value" of switching that dominates the convenience of auto-ship. Consequently, firms cannot rely on consumer "laziness" (search frictions) to sustain lock-in when supply chains are unstable. Second, competitive effects are non-monotone: adding an auto-ship option can paradoxically soften price competition via segmentation, whereas greater differentiation or higher search frictions can intensify rivalry. Finally, we show that symmetric dual-mode adoption can simultaneously boost firm profits and consumer surplus.

title: Working Conditions in Light of Factory Law Provisions of the Public Sector Enterprises of Bangladesh: A Case Study on Jute Mills
