detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of sampling schemes on Monte Carlo-based Value-at-Risk (VaR) estimation at both the risk factor and portfolio levels. We compare pseudo-random number generators with low-discrepancy sequences, including Sobol and Halton constructions. At the uncorrelated risk factor level, pseudo-random generators exhibit higher variability and less stable VaR estimates than low-discrepancy sequences. When correlation is introduced, the differences between the generators in how closely the theoretical VaR is achieved are substantially reduced. Moreover, portfolio aggregation further diminishes these differences, while the accuracy with which the theoretical VaR is represented also decreases across all generators. Optimized Sobol sequences (Sobol OPT and Sobol EN) demonstrate superior preservation of correlation structures, particularly in higher-dimensional settings. Overall, the results highlight the role of advanced random number generation techniques in enhancing the efficiency and reliability of VaR estimation in portfolio risk management.

title: Towards Low-Carbon Buildings: Optimizing Hydrogen Integrated Energy Systems and Coordinating EV-HFCV Management
affiliations: North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, China University of Petroleum (Huadong) and University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Towards Low-Carbon Buildings: Optimizing Hydrogen Integrated Energy Systems and Coordinating EV-HFCV Management
detail.abstract: The low-carbon operation of building integrated energy systems (BIES) are pivotal for decarbonizing urban buildings while maintaining occupant comfort. This study proposes a lowcarbon operation framework for a BIES that couples electricity, heating, cooling, hydrogen and virtual storage with a multi-energy storage portfolio. To reflect hydrogen's practical role in building decarbonization, diversified hydrogen utilization pathways are explicitly modeled within the BIES. To achieve joint carbon reduction in the building and transportation sectors, a BIES low-carbon operation model is constructed by comprehensively considering the electricity and hydrogen energy demands of electric vehicles and hydrogen-fueled vehicles, with the objectives of economic efficiency, environmental sustainability, and independence. Uncertainties in photovoltaic generation and building loads are addressed using a moment-based distributionally robust chance-constrained formulation to improve reliability while maximizing its economic efficiency. The research results show that: (1) Diversified utilization of hydrogen energy in BIES reduces operational costs and carbon emissions by 10.03% and 21.24%, respectively. (2) A multi-energy storage system configuration results in a 13.58% reduction in operational costs, a 0.84% reduction in carbon emissions, and a 3.57% increase in independence. (3) Compared to operating them independently, coordinated electric vehicles and hydrogen-fueled vehicles scheduling reduces costs by 4.02% and carbon emissions by 3.25%. The proposed approach provides actionable insights for low-carbon and resilient building energy management with integrated hydrogen and mobility services.

title: Can the Government Get People to Have More Babies?
affiliations: KIPF (Korea Institute of Public Finance) and KIPF (Korea Institute of Public Finance)

detail.title: Can the Government Get People to Have More Babies?
detail.abstract: We study the fertility effects of central and local pronatalist cash transfers in South Korea. Using population-wide administrative records from the National Health Insurance Service, we exploit sharp eligibility and announcement cutoffs from the 2023 expansion of the universal Parental Allowance and estimate short-run effects using a regression-discontinuity differencein-differences design. We find declines in births at thresholds, with larger effects among older and lower-income women, and no evidence of short-run adjustments in birth order or delivery type. Local lump-sum baby bonuses generate modest fertility gains, concentrated in non-capital areas and driven by parity-specific bonus schedules rather than broader quasi-cash benefits.

title: Pairs Trading in Crypto
affiliations: Cornell Financial Engineering Manhattan, , Cornell University, Cornell University, Cornell University and Cornell University

detail.title: Pairs Trading in Crypto
detail.abstract: We develop an automated framework for cryptocurrency pairs trading that identifies stable relationships across assets and executes mean reversion strategies in real time. Using 2 years of hourly data for more than 500 coins, we construct a multi-stage selection process that combines correlation clustering, structural metadata, and stability diagnostics to isolate pairs with persistent relative value behavior. We implement these signals through the Hummingbot platform, where we fine tune entry thresholds, holding rules, and risk controls before deploying the strategy in live markets. Through extensive backtesting and live trading on selected pairs, we show that our funnel improves signal quality, enhances stability across regimes, and produces consistent market neutral returns while revealing important challenges related to liquidity, convergence reliability, and execution costs.

title: Population Aging and Monetary Policy Effectiveness: Age-Dependent Consumption and the Declining Transmission of Interest Rates - A Life-Cycle DSGE Analysis

detail.title: Population Aging and Monetary Policy Effectiveness: Age-Dependent Consumption and the Declining Transmission of Interest Rates - A Life-Cycle DSGE Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper develops a life-cycle overlapping generations DSGE model to analyze how population aging diminishes monetary policy eectiveness. The key insight is that consumption patterns exhibit systematic age variation: working-age households have high marginal propensity to consume (MPC) from current income and respond strongly to interest rate changes, while elderly retirees have lower MPC and consumption tied to accumulated wealth rather than income. As populations age, the share of interest-rate-sensitive consumers declines, attenuating monetary transmission. We build a tractable three-period OLG model with young workers, middle-aged savers, and elderly retirees, embedded in a New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities. Calibrated to match demographic transitions in Japan (elderly share rising from 20% in 2000 to 35% in 2040), the model generates three key results. First, the consumption response to a 100 basis point interest rate shock declines by 45% as the economy ages, with aggregate MPC falling from 0.62 to 0.34.

title: Fiscal-Based Monetary Policy Rules - Beyond Inflation Targeting: Interest Rates as Fiscal Stabilization Tools

detail.title: Fiscal-Based Monetary Policy Rules - Beyond Inflation Targeting: Interest Rates as Fiscal Stabilization Tools
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel monetary policy framework where interest rates respond directly to scal variables rather than ination. We propose the Fiscal Stabilization Rule (FSR), where the central bank sets rates based on government spending growth, debt dynamics, and output gapscompletely abandoning ination targeting. This represents a fundamental departure from the Taylor rule paradigm that has dominated monetary economics for three decades. The theoretical foundation rests on scal-monetary coordination: when scal policy becomes the primary demand stabilization tool, monetary policy optimally supports scal sustainability by adjusting borrowing costs. We embed the FSR in a complete DSGE model with: (i) government spending as the main cyclical stabilizer, (ii) endogenous debt dynamics, (iii) distortionary taxation, and (iv) nominal rigidities. The model yields closed-form solutions for optimal interest rate responses to scal variables. Quantitative analysis reveals that FSR-based policy achieves superior macroeconomic stabilization compared to Taylor rules when scal shocks dominate. A 1% increase in government spending triggers a 25 basis point rate increase under the Fiscal-Based Monetary Policy Dr Gazi Arif FSR, preventing debt spirals while accommodating necessary scal expansion. The framework performs especially well in: (1) high-debt economies where scal sustainability concerns dominate, (2) supply-shock environments where ination targeting creates perverse outcomes, and (3) developing countries with weak ination-output relationships. Policy simulations demonstrate that FSR can reduce output volatility by 15-30% relative to ination targeting in scally-stressed economies. However, the rule requires strong scal disciplinewithout credible spending commitments, FSR degenerates into scal dominance. We derive necessary conditions for FSR stability and characterize the scal-monetary coordination equilibrium. The analysis provides practical guidance for central banks in high-debt environments considering alternatives to conventional ination targeting.

title: Dialectical History of Social Production

detail.title: Dialectical History of Social Production
detail.abstract: This work presents a critical and rigorous interpretation of the history of modes of production through historical materialism. From primitive community to slavery, feudalism, capitalism, and socialism, it analyzes how productive forces and social relations of production evolve through internal contradictions. Drawing on Marx and Engels, it shows that every economic system is historical, transitory, and shaped by dialectical tensions that drive social transformation.

title: Monetary Policy with Constraints: A Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Analysis With Complete Model Derivations

detail.title: Monetary Policy with Constraints: A Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Analysis With Complete Model Derivations
detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) model to investigate how collateral constraints and nancial intermediation shape the eectiveness of monetary policy. The model integrates a central bank implementing a modied Taylor rule with borrowing-constrained representative agents and an endogenous nancial sector. It accounts for both lower bounds (zero lower bound) and upper bounds on nominal interest rates, and embeds debt constraints that evolve with stochastic shocks to borrowing capacity. Government debt dynamics and scal interactions are explicitly modeled. Our ndings highlight that under binding borrowing constraints, the transmission of monetary policy is attenuated, particularly near constraint boundaries. Moreover, increases in government debt weaken the central bank's ability to stabilize output through interest rate rules alone. The model reveals that monetary policy eectiveness depends not only on traditional output and ination gaps but also on debt ratios and credit supply conditions. These results challenge the suciency of conventional interest rate rules in nancially constrained economies and underscore the importance of coordinated scal-monetary policy frameworks.

title: What Does “By Object”, in Effect, Mean? In Search for the Ultimate Determination Criterion
affiliations: Comenius University in Bratislava, Faculty of Law

detail.title: What Does “By Object”, in Effect, Mean? In Search for the Ultimate Determination Criterion

publicationDetails.detailsText: Market and Competition Law Review, Volume ix, No. 2, October 2025, pp. 37-68

detail.abstract:
This article is dedicated to an EU competition law evergreen – by object restrictions. The CJEU established in its early case law that Article 101(1) TFEU (or its predecessors) could be infringed by restricting competition (i) by object or (ii) by effect. Once the former is present, the latter does not have to be. In other words, if an agreement restricts competition by object, it is superfluous to analyse and prove the actual restrictive effects on competition. The concept seems simple, yet it is far from it. As many other concepts, the concept of by object restrictions has developed with time. We believe that the last dozen of years has shown a particularly interesting development; recent judgements, delivered in 2023 and 2024, being no exception. It seems that the borderline between by object and by effect restriction is getting blurred and the whole concept of by object restriction more elusive, to the detriment of public as well as private enforcement of competition law. 

Thus, this article asks: which criteria are used in classification of a restriction as a by object one? Is there any ultimate criterion which is the most decisive in the classification process? 

In order to answer the questions, the article dives into case law on restrictions of competition by object. A qualitative analysis of selected (landmark) cases from Allianz Hungaria (2013) to recent judgements is conducted. The factual background of the analysed cases is presented briefly. The focus of the analysis is on the identification of criteria used by the CJEU when determining whether a restriction of competition is a by object one. The CJEU often repeats the same criteria, however, in certain cases it also adds new criteria which may (but not always are) repeated in the subsequent case law. Therefore, the qualitative analysis leads to the identification of a spectrum of criteria. Moreover, since the analysis is qualitative and not merely statistic, it also leads to the answer to the question what is, pursuant to the CJEU, the essential criterion in determination of whether a competition is restricted by object.

title: A Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Model with Asset Prices and Financial Markets

detail.title: A Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium Model with Asset Prices and Financial Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model that explicitly incorporates asset prices and financial market dynamics. The framework extends the standard Real Business Cycle model by introducing equity markets, portfolio choice, and capital adjustment costs. Households optimize over consumption, labor supply, government bonds, and equity holdings, while firms face capital accumulation decisions governed by Tobin's Q. The model features three stochastic disturbances: technology shocks, monetary policy innovations, and asset valuation (sentiment) shocks. We derive analytical solutions for the steady state, perform log-linearization for numerical analysis, and characterize the dynamic responses to various shocks. The model successfully generates realistic asset price volatility, equity premia, and co-movement between financial variables and real activity. Applications include analyzing wealth effects, the transmission mechanism of monetary policy through asset prices, and the role of financial market sentiment in business cycle fluctuations.

title: Private Enforcement of Eu Competition Law - How to Kill Stand-alone Actions in Slovak Style

detail.abstract: EU competition law may be enforced in two ways: public enforcement via competition authorities (such as the European Commission or the Antimonopoly Office of the Slovak Republic) or private enforcement via actions for damages on national courts. The latter enforcement was supposed to be stimulated by Damages Directive (2014/104/EU),which was implemented on the Slovak level by Act No. 350/2016 Coll. Private actions for damages caused by infringements of competition law in the EU are far from frequent, especially within Slovakia. There are undisputably various causes for this, not all of thembeing legal. This contribution presents one particular legal cause for this struggle which have national roots, i.e. the impossibility of stand-alone actions for damages in Slovakia. The aim of this contribution is to show how stand-alone actions for damages are hindered by interpretation of procedural rules of the Slovak procedural code, thus leaving enforcement of competition law ineffective.

title: Finding Alpha in Diversity: Data-Driven Insights from Structural change in Japanese Firms
affiliations: Blackrock, BlackRock, Inc - San Francisco, BlackRock, Inc - San Francisco and BlackRock, Inc

detail.title: Finding Alpha in Diversity: Data-Driven Insights from Structural change in Japanese Firms
detail.abstract:
Aided by advanced technology and rich firm level data, we can now distinguish Japanese companies along dimensions that matter directly for long term value creation. The first is shareholder orientation. Some firms are actively dismantling legacy cross-shareholding networks, while others remain tied to “stable” ownership structures and muted market discipline.

The second is labor and staffing resilience. In an economy with a shrinking working age population and already high participation, headcount is hard to expand quickly. Many firms instead adjust through hours worked and overtime. New evidence from labor statistics and employee reviews allows us to see which companies are using this margin to serve strong demand and which are simply stretching staff. The third is how well companies harness under-represented talent, especially younger workers and women in boards and management. We focus on whether such people hold real decision-making roles, the depth and stability of that representation, and how it aligns with Japan’s push for more inclusive governance.

title: Taxing AI
affiliations: University of Georgia School of Law

detail.title: Taxing AI
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to transform the distribution and sources of income, with some experts predicting widespread job displacement. Even under optimistic projections, AI is expected to exacerbate wealth inequality, given that the technology’s ownership and immense value are concentrated within a subset of Big Tech companies and AI startups. These outcomes will have far-reaching impacts on the federal tax system, which heavily relies on taxing individual labor income and payroll, rather than capital or consumption.

This Article argues that AI threatens to disrupt the tax system’s ability to fulfill its fundamental goals of raising revenue, redistributing income, and regulating taxpayer behavior. The risk is heightened by the federal government’s dependence on individual labor income, even as economic value shifts toward mobile capital and AI ownership by large firms. The Article proposes two interventions to help address these challenges. In the short term, it recommends increasing the capital gains rates on the sale of ownership interests in AI-intensive firms. This approach would primarily serve to internalize the distributive imbalances generated by wealth concentration in AI firms. In the long term, the Article suggests adopting a broad-based consumption tax if the share of labor income declines. This proposal would represent a more drastic change, aimed at rebalancing a tax system that can no longer depend on taxing individual labor income.

detail.abstract: This expanded working paper examines the use of legal instruments and normative narratives in the context of maritime disputes in the Aegean Sea, with particular focus on the applicable framework of public international law governing continental shelf and exclusive economic zone entitlements. Drawing upon the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the Charter of the United Nations, the Treaties of Lausanne (1923) and Paris (1947), the Montreux Convention (1936), as well as relevant United Nations principles and state practice, the paper evaluates the legal consistency of competing maritime claims advanced in the region. Particular attention is devoted to recent doctrinal narratives and bilateral arrangements assessed in light of binding international legal norms. The study concludes that the legal rights exercised by Greece derive ipso facto et ab initio from international law and reflect obligations and entitlements applicable erga omnes.

detail.abstract: Australia’s energy transition is often framed as a generation challenge, yet the primary constraint is national infrastructure coordination. This report presents a systems level framework for planning Australia’s future energy architecture across generation, storage, transmission, and digital grid management. It evaluates structural weaknesses in current planning arrangements and proposes an integrated national model that aligns engineering requirements with long term investment strategy and governance reform. Technical considerations include grid modernisation, distributed energy integration, storage deployment, and the role of intelligent network control in maintaining reliability under high renewable penetration. Economic analysis explores capital allocation pathways, risk distribution, and the need for coordinated infrastructure sequencing to avoid bottlenecks and stranded assets. The report argues that without a unified infrastructure strategy, Australia risks higher transition costs, reliability pressures, and missed industrial opportunities. The framework is intended to inform policymakers, infrastructure planners, regulators, and private investors engaged in shaping Australia’s energy future.

title: The Mirage of Resilience: Targeted Fiscal Stimulus, Data Lags, and the Systemic Risks of Monetary Over-Tightening (2025–2026)
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Mirage of Resilience: Targeted Fiscal Stimulus, Data Lags, and the Systemic Risks of Monetary Over-Tightening (2025–2026)
detail.abstract:
This study seeks to deconstruct the severe divergence between U.S. macroeconomic data performance in early 2026 and the Federal Reserve's (Fed) monetary policy trajectory. Through a penetrating analysis of the manufacturing PMI and the commercial real estate (CRE) credit market, the paper presents the following core findings: 
First, the marginal expansion in the U.S. manufacturing PMI in early 2026 (e.g., 51.9 in January) is fundamentally driven by targeted capital expenditure (Targeted CapEx) propelled by the CHIPS and Science Act and AI infrastructure initiatives. Such administratively directed investments exhibit significant immunity to interest rate adjustments, statistically masking a deep recession in the broader civilian industrial sector.
Second, this study identifies the “Data Lag Trap”. The Fed’s reliance on lagged indicators— particularly the shelter component of CPI and employment metrics—exhibits pronounced backward-looking characteristics. Empirical evidence shows that while real-time market rents have recorded consecutive negative growth, the official statistics’ inherent lag has confined policymakers to a cognitive blind spot of “rearview mirror navigation”, resulting in the maintenance of unnecessarily tight policy during a phase of economic deceleration.
Finally, the paper exposes systemic vulnerabilities in regional banks during a “valuation silence” period. It highlights that CRE concentration ratios at certain regional banks have exceeded 600% of equity capital, with balance-sheet stability artificially sustained through deferred revaluation amid severely depressed transaction volumes. If the Fed persists in ignoring this policy inertia rooted in distorted data, it will inevitably precipitate a nonlinear crisis jointly driven by credit collapse and social unrest.
The conclusion posits that current monetary policy has deviated from data-driven science and evolved into an intertemporal power game. Policymakers should immediately correct their dependence on “polluted data” and implement preemptive rate cuts to mitigate impending structural ruptures.

title: Deadlocked in History and Geopolitics: Revisiting Armenia-Turkey Relations
affiliations: American University of Armenia

detail.title: Deadlocked in History and Geopolitics: Revisiting Armenia-Turkey Relations

publicationDetails.detailsText: Digest of Middle East Studies, volume 30, issue 3, 2021[10.1111/dome.12242 ]

detail.abstract:
Located at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, Armenia and Turkey are two neighboring countries that share a 311 km of land border. Official relations between them, however, remain antagonistic as they never established diplomatic relations, and the land border remains closed. All the past efforts to normalize relations and eradicate the standoff have foundered. This article engages with several methodological problems and (mis)perceptions that persist in existing interpretations of Armenia–Turkey relations and examines their impact on the current deadlock. It particularly discusses the questions of the closed border, its relevance to the conflict in Karabakh, the importance of disentangling the process of normalization from reconciliation, and its impact on past normalization initiatives. The article argues that critical rethinking of several deep seated conceptions and approaches

could expand our understanding about the roots of the present rift and propose avenues for resolving the impasse.

title: When Refugees Enter Through the Main Door: Geography of Electoral Backlash under Temporary Protection in Poland

publicationDetails.detailsText: Centro Studi Luca d'Agliano Development Studies Working Paper No. 511
publicationDetails.journalName: Centro Studi Luca d'Agliano Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We leverage the massive inflow of Ukrainian refugees in Poland after the start of the large-scale Ukrainian-Russian conflict (2022), the largest humanitarian crisis in a European country since World War II, to investigate potential electoral backlashes under the best-case scenario in which the reception system is fully designed for refugee integration (i.e., under EU Temporary Protection). We employ a novel measure of refugees (the share of Ukrainian primary school students in Polish schools), which can better capture refugees' location at a granular (municipal) level compared to alternative measures adopted in previous studies. Our difference-indifferences event-study analysis based on parliamentary and presidential elections held since 2019 shows that Ukrainian refugee inflows increased local support for a mainstream conservative party, while simultaneously reducing the propensity to support more radical alternative-right parties. Drawing on established interdisciplinary scholarship, we discuss potential mechanisms underlying these effects.

publicationDetails.detailsText: De Nederlandsche Bank Working Paper No. 854
publicationDetails.journalName: De Nederlandsche Bank Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Regulatory limits on intragroup exposures constrain capital allocation within multi-national banking groups. We develop a theoretical model of cross-border banking that captures internal capital markets under supranational supervision and borrowing constraints. Our analysis shows that relaxing intragroup exposure limits can amplify risk-taking by enabling parent banks to draw on affiliate resources and reallocate risk toward the home market, particularly when foreign affiliates are large, well capitalized, and subject to weaker liquidity requirements. We characterize the conditions under which this channel operates and discuss its implications for financial stability. Our findings inform the debate on multinational banking groups by showing how risks can emerge within these organizations and how regulatory tools can mitigate them.

detail.abstract: This study provides a critical re-evaluation of India's engagement in BRICS energy governance, focusing on the structural rupture caused by the "October Shock" in late 2025. It argues that India's strategic autonomy, initially characterized by record opportunistic purchases of discounted Russian crude, was fundamentally a function of Western permissiveness that evaporated with the U.S. Treasury's designation of Rosneft and Lukoil as Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs) on October 22, 2025. Utilizing the theoretical frameworks of Status Inconsistency and Weaponized Interdependence, the analysis identifies a "compliance pivot" within India's corporate sector, specifically at Reliance Industries, which halted Russian imports for its SEZ refinery on November 20, 2025, to protect $15 billion in annual Western export revenue. The findings demonstrate that India's BRICS engagement has bifurcated into a rhetorical domain of "Symbolic Solidarity" and a material domain of "Forced Compliance." The study concludes that while BRICS remains a vital lever for managing India's status aspirations, its utility as a material shield against Western financial weaponry was empirically pierced by the secondary sanctions regime of 2025.

title: Do Oil Price Shocks Help or Hurt Growth? Asymmetric Evidence from Jordan (2008-2023)
affiliations: University of Jordan

detail.title: Do Oil Price Shocks Help or Hurt Growth? Asymmetric Evidence from Jordan (2008-2023)
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether oil price increases and decreases affect economic growth symmetrically in a net oil-importing economy, using Jordan as a case study over 2008Q2-2023Q3. Quarterly real GDP growth is paired with Brent crude prices, and oil shocks are constructed as log changes and decomposed into positive and negative components following Mork (1989). The relationship is estimated using OLS with four quarterly lags, complemented by a general-to-specific (GETS) reduction and standard diagnostic and stability checks. The results show a positive and statistically significant association between aggregate oil shocks and growth (about 0.03%), while positive oil shocks are not statistically significant. In contrast, negative oil shocks exhibit a positive and statistically significant effect on growth (about 0.05%), indicating an asymmetric growth response to oil price movements in Jordan. Policy implications emphasize leveraging periods of declining oil prices to support priority investment spending, stimulate private investment in less oil-sensitive sectors, and accelerate investment in energy alternatives and renewables, supported by a dedicated governmental unit to monitor and forecast global oil prices.

title: Methods to Tailor Behavioural Interventions: A Systematic Review of Categorisation Approaches in (Energy) Economics
affiliations: , University College Dublin, Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt,  and

detail.title: Methods to Tailor Behavioural Interventions: A Systematic Review of Categorisation Approaches in (Energy) Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Dutch Research Council (NWO): NWA.1389.20.251.

detail.abstract: Transitioning to clean energy is necessary to meet the climate targets of the Paris Agreement. Accelerating decarbonisation requires improving energy efficiency and making large-scale green energy investments, inter alia in residential homes. Household energy behaviours and investment decisions are mostly suboptimal as individuals often face significant psychological barriers and are subjected to cognitive biases. Consequently, one-size-fits-all interventions, that are aimed at fostering green energy behaviours, lead to information overload and rebound effects, thereby being inefficient. A growing proposition in behavioural sciences is to personalise the delivery of behavioural interventions (BIs) to facilitate the uptake of energy-efficient behaviours. This is typically done, for example, by tailoring different BIs to individuals to overcome individual biases in the adoption of green appliances and renovations. Nonetheless, there is no clear know-how to use different statistical methods to tailor BIs. While researchers rely on various techniques to customise BIs for specific groups, this segmentation process lacks coherence overall. In this paper, we systematically review and sort the literature on statistical classification and clustering models, including machine learning methods, that have been used to optimise BIs for improving residential energy efficiency. Our review provides a holistic overview of these different methods, along with recommendations for practitioners to use them. It further highlights the role that machine learning algorithms can play in automating BIs, for example, by using sophisticated data analysis and pattern recognition to identify intricate relationships between decision-making factors. These insights can lead to highly optimised personalised strategies for increased energy efficiency.

title: When Equilibrium Exists but Cannot Be Implemented
affiliations: and Texas Tech University

detail.title: When Equilibrium Exists but Cannot Be Implemented
detail.abstract: Classical equilibrium theory guarantees the existence of equilibrium under minimal assumptions on preferences and technology. These results, however, implicitly presume that economic agents can compute and implement equilibrium actions without cognitive or computational constraints. This paper revisits the equilibrium concept by explicitly incorporating finite computational rationality. We define an Implementable Competitive Equilibrium (ICE) as a competitive equilibrium supported by decentralized polynomial-time decision procedures that map market signals (prices and endowments) into exact Walrasian demands. We show that there exist competitive economies with standard convexity/continuity properties but implicitly described feasibility constraints in which an Arrow-Debreu equilibrium exists, yet no ICE exists under any reasonable computational constraint. The impossibility result arises not from behavioral frictions, information imperfections, or approximation, but from the intrinsic computational hardness of individual optimization and consistency conditions under compact representations. Our findings suggest that equilibrium existence alone is insufficient for economic relevance and call for a reconsideration of equilibrium as an implementable object rather than a purely mathematical construct.

title: Attention is Money: How Digital Distraction Makes Retail Investors Take More Risks

detail.title: Attention is Money: How Digital Distraction Makes Retail Investors Take More Risks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known personal or financial conflicts of interest that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a conceptual and theoretical analysis based on existing literature and does not involve human participants, primary data collection, experiments, or identifiable personal data. Therefore, ethics approval was not required.

detail.abstract: Today's investment apps use games and social media to get people to trade. This causes a problem for old ideas about how smart people make financial decisions. Traditional finance thinks investors can fully focus and process all information, but modern digital life makes it hard for people to focus. This paper looks at how attention, which we call a valuable type of psychological resource, affects how much risk investors take on distracting, easy-to-use digital platforms. We use ideas from Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, along with current ideas about constant partial attention. The main mental problems we study are: 1) a stronger "availability heuristic" (where you believe things happen more often because you see them a lot) caused by social media, and 2) how distracting design stops the necessary deep thinking ('System 2' processing) needed to research investments. We find that always seeing quick, big-win stories makes investors wrongly think that big, unlikely rewards are more probable. This constant lack of focus changes how investors decide on risk. The result is that regulators need to quickly look at how platforms are designed, especially features that use up limited focus to make regular investors trade more often and take bigger risks.

title: Stablecoins and Tokenized Assets: Impact on Derivatve Counterparty Credit Risk

detail.title: Stablecoins and Tokenized Assets: Impact on Derivatve Counterparty Credit Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No Applicable

detail.abstract:
The increasing use of payment stablecoins for payments and settlements in financial transactions and the tokenization of financial assets, presents new opportunities for efficiency, especially when these assets are employed as collateral in derivative transactions. These technological advancements can significantly reduce delays in three critical areas: the valuation of collateral, the process of posting and receiving collateral, and the final settlement of collateral. As a result of these accelerated processes, the margin period of risk (MPOR)—the period in which the value of collateral and the value of the reference portfolio may move apart—is expected to decline. A shorter MPOR indicates that the gap between the value of the portfolio and its collateral at any point, including at the time of default, becomes smaller. This compression of the MPOR leads to a reduction in widely used measures of counterparty credit risk exposure, such as exposure at default and the credit valuation adjustment (CVA). Ultimately, these changes promote stronger risk management practices and enhance overall market efficiency.

For example, if payment stablecoins—backed one-for-one by assets like cash or U.S. Treasuries as required under the 2025 Genius Act—are accepted as eligible financial collateral for over-the-counter (OTC) derivative transactions, standard MPOR thresholds (such as the typical 10 business days for OTC derivatives) may be reconsidered and potentially reduced to better reflect these operational improvements.

This paper examines various scenarios illustrating the impact of using payment stablecoins and tokenized financial assets on counterparty credit risk exposure, considering different assumptions for the MPOR. Estimates suggest that shortening the MPOR from 10 business days to 5 business days could decrease counterparty credit risk in derivative transactions by as much as 29%. Such a reduction would provide substantial capital efficiencies for U.S. Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs).

title: The Conceptual Foundations of Self-Control and its Link to Impulsivity and Attention
affiliations: School of Economics, University of Sydney, The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney - School of Economics and Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT) University

detail.title: The Conceptual Foundations of Self-Control and its Link to Impulsivity and Attention

detail.abstract: Self-control, attention, and impulsivity jointly support goal-directed behavior yet are often examined in isolation with heterogeneous measures. We integrate validated self-reported scales with a hybrid, incentivized behavioral task that synthesizes two canonical experimental designs and adds novel extensions to measure these constructs in a typical work context. Using data from a preregistered four-session online study (N = 443 adults), we characterize the cross-relationships and the relationships between different measures of self-control, attention, and impulsivity and evaluate their contributions to effort allocation over time. More broadly, the study advances an emerging research program that leverages laboratory settings with well-structured economic incentives to examine the role of personality traits and cognitive limitations in economic decision making.

title: The Impact of State-Level R&D Incentives Versus Educational Attainment on Innovation
affiliations: Providence College

detail.title: The Impact of State-Level R&D Incentives Versus Educational Attainment on Innovation
detail.abstract: The 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a provision allowing for immediate expensing of research and development (R&D) expenditures. States are deciding whether they should match this change or retain their current R&D write-off policy. This paper uses state-level panel data from 2013 to 2019 to examine whether state extramural R&D expenditure or educational attainment has a more economically significant association with innovation, proxied by annual state-level patent counts. Using a year fixed-effects negative binomial regression model, the results suggest that, while both variables have a statistically significant positive relationship with patent counts, educational attainment has a more economically significant relationship than state extramural R&D expenditure.

title: The Impact of Weather on U.S. Agricultural Capacity Utilization: A Multiple-Output Nonparametric Analysis
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Impact of Weather on U.S. Agricultural Capacity Utilization: A Multiple-Output Nonparametric Analysis
detail.abstract: This study uses a state-level dataset from 1960 to 2015 and employs a nonparametric data envelopment analysis (DEA) approach to investigate how weather conditions affect agricultural capacity utilization. We estimate capacity utilization using a short-run ray average cost minimization model within a production technology framework that incorporates multiple outputs (Crops, Livestock and products, and Farm related output) produced from multiple variable inputs and multiple fixed inputs (Capital, and Land), following the method introduced by Ray, Walden, and Chen (2021). The findings indicate that most states operated below full capacity and exhibit systematic regional patterns. A second-stage two-way fixed effect model reveals that weather conditions significantly contribute to the shortfall in capacity utilization.

title: Ad-driven Quality Degradation on E-commerce Platforms: A Theory and Empirical Strategy
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Ad-driven Quality Degradation on E-commerce Platforms: A Theory and Empirical Strategy
detail.abstract: We develop a formal theory of how paid visibility (advertising and paid ranking) on multi-sided e-commerce platforms can drive a systemic shift toward low-quality and falsely advertised products. Building on information asymmetry, reputation dynamics, and platform revenue incentives, we show mathematically that when platform visibility is sufficiently dominated by paid factors, the marginal return to investments in real quality and long-term reputation falls below the return to investments in short-term promotional signaling or deceptive listings. This produces a tipping threshold: above a critical paid-visibility weight, the market equilibrium is dominated by low-quality or falsely advertised sellers-a quality-reversal equilibrium. We derive conditions for the threshold, characterize comparative statics, and discuss empirical identification strategies (including image-similarity detection, event-study exploitation of platform policy changes, and difference-indifferences designs). The model yields testable predictions and direct policy implications for platform governance and regulation.

title: Disequilibrium Inflation

The model demonstrates that Taylor Rules are effective when the inflation rate moves to the same direction with regard to money as a medium of exchange and a storage of value. Under deflation, these two functions of money diverge oppositely and that leads to a liquidity trap which the economy struggles to escape.

title: Ethics as Compression
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Ethics as Compression
