detail.abstract: We propose a mechanistic framework treating ethics as a compression mechanism for cognition and enforcement in complex cooperation systems. Rising cooperation complexity C induces rule explosion R, which in turn drives increases in ethical abstraction level E (principles, meta-rights, meta-procedures) to reduce decision and enforcement costs. However, institutionalization of ethics amplifies downstream capture K, nested conflicts, and rule/semantic inflation, raising conflict cost X. This triggers either meta-abstraction upgrades E ₁ or failure modes ₙ₊ (fragmentation, undergroundization, coercive resets). We formalize the loop as 16 testable laws and extend it with "risk ethics" (inoculation, budgeting, zero-risk paradox, capacity-first), explaining why overprotection can increase tail risks. We conclude with falsifiable predictions and empirical research agendas.

title: Geoeconomic Imperatives of Ethiopia's Quest for Red Sea Port Access: An Institutional Economics Perspective
affiliations: Oda Bultum University

detail.title: Geoeconomic Imperatives of Ethiopia's Quest for Red Sea Port Access: An Institutional Economics Perspective
detail.abstract: Ethiopia's quest for Red Sea port access exemplifies the intersection of historical legacies, legal frameworks, and contemporary geoeconomic imperatives. Since Eritrea's independence in 1993, Ethiopia's landlocked status has imposed significant transaction costs, foreign-exchange leakage, and strategic dependency on Djibouti. While prevailing narratives emphasize escalation and sovereignty disputes, this paper reframes the issue through institutional economics, highlighting rules, incentives, and governance structures as pathways to de-escalation, commercialization, and mutual benefit. By analyzing historical foundations, current claims, media narratives, and underexplored geoeconomic imperatives, the study proposes institutional pathways-contracts, escrow mechanisms, arbitration, and phased pilots-that can depoliticize maritime access and transform contested ports into engines of shared prosperity and regional stability.

title: Decarbonizing a Portfolio of Operating Assets: Cost Estimates for Vehicle Fleets
affiliations: University of Mannheim - Business School, University of Mannheim and University of Mannheim - Business School

detail.title: Decarbonizing a Portfolio of Operating Assets: Cost Estimates for Vehicle Fleets

publicationDetails.detailsText: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series No. 223
publicationDetails.journalName: TRR 266 Accounting for Transparency Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Companies across industries seek to assess the costs of complying with environmental regulations and meeting voluntary emission targets. This paper develops a carbon abatement cost model for firms operating a portfolio of assets with differing cost or load profiles. The resulting abatement cost curves serve as a decision tool for configuring individual assets to achieve firm-wide emission reductions at least cost. We apply our model to urban bus fleets regulated under the California Cap-and-Trade Program. We find that a carbon price of $35 per ton of CO2e (2024 average) incentivizes firms to configure their fleets such that battery-electric drivetrains constitute 70% of usable installed capacity and 92% of annual demand, while diesel drivetrains serve peak loads. Since the resulting emissions are fairly inelastic to the carbon price, we conclude that the life-cycle cost per mile would increase substantially if deep decarbonization were to be induced entirely by higher carbon prices.

title: Looser, Tighter, Clearer: A New Financial Conditions Index for the Euro Area
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB), European Central Bank (ECB) and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Looser, Tighter, Clearer: A New Financial Conditions Index for the Euro Area
detail.abstract: Financial Conditions Indices (FCIs) are a widely used tool for assessing the broader monetary policy stance beyond the central bank’s direct control. This paper presents a novel vector autoregressive (VAR) model that includes key macroeconomic variables and maps financial variables into a single index, named Macro-Finance FCI. The VAR coefficients and the FCI weights are estimated jointly in one step, ensuring a model-consistent microfinance feedback. The model-implied long-run mean of the index provides a neutral benchmark to which financial conditions converge when inflation is at target and output is at potential. For the euro area, the proposed FCI incorporates nine asset prices – including risk-free rates, sovereign spreads, risk assets, and the exchange rate – and assigns a dominant role to nominal interest rates. It outperforms existing indices in out-of-sample forecasts of inflation and output. A structural identification of supply, demand, and financial shocks indicates that financial conditions require up to one year to transmit to the real economy and almost up to two years to inflation.

title: Hub Only Pipeline Topology Architecture Standard (HOPT-AS)
affiliations: Novonanmek Material Sciences Private Limited

detail.title: Hub Only Pipeline Topology Architecture Standard (HOPT-AS)
detail.abstract:
The Hub-Only Pipeline Topology Architecture Standard (HOPT-AS) v1.0 defines a governed, system-level architecture for large-scale carbon capture, transport, and storage (CCUS) in regions where conventional emitter-to-pipeline models are economically, logistically, or regulatorily constrained. The standard formalizes the Hub-Only Pipeline Topology (HOPT), an architectural approach in which industrial emitters capture CO₂ in solid-bound form and interface exclusively through solids-based logistics, while all gaseous CO₂ handling, conditioning, compression, and pipeline injection occur at centralized regeneration hubs. CO₂ pipelines therefore connect only hubs to hubs and onward to storage or utilization, eliminating direct emitter–pipeline connectivity.

HOPT-AS establishes mandatory topology rules, system boundaries, stakeholder roles, and participation constraints to ensure interoperability, scalability, and architectural integrity across multi-stakeholder deployments. The standard defines hub and emitter classes, permitted topology families, governance and certification mechanisms, registry-based chain-of-custody, and a structured framework for monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV). It is technology-neutral with respect to capture chemistry and detailed engineering design, focusing instead on architectural consistency, governance, and repeatable deployment models.

By relocating gaseous CO₂ handling from emitters to shared hubs, HOPT-AS lowers entry barriers for small and medium emitters, reduces total pipeline length and permitting complexity, and enables phased deployment using existing logistics infrastructure. The standard is intended for reference, design alignment, pilot deployment, early adoption, and future certification by industry, governments, regulators, financiers, and infrastructure developers seeking scalable CCUS systems in distributed industrial regions.

title: Macroeconomic Effects Of Carbon-intensive Energy Price Changes: A Model Comparison
affiliations: Swiss National Bank, , Central Bank of Chile, , European Central Bank (ECB), Deutsche Bundesbank, , Banco de España, Deutsche Bundesbank and European Union - Directorate General for Economic and Financial Affairs (DG ECFIN)

detail.title: Macroeconomic Effects Of Carbon-intensive Energy Price Changes: A Model Comparison
detail.abstract: This paper presents a novel model comparison to examine the challenges posed by changes in carbon-intensive energy prices for monetary policy. The employed environmental monetary models have a detailed multi-sector structure. The comparison assesses the effects of both a temporary and a permanent energy price increase with a particular focus on the euro area and the United States. Temporary and permanent price shocks are both inflationary. However, the inflationary impact of the permanent shock depends on the underlying model assumptions and monetary policy response. The analysis also establishes that these models share large commonalities in their quantitative and qualitative results, while also pointing out cross-country differences.

title: Industrial Policy as Market-Shaping Competition: Evidence from China, the European Union, and the United States (2009-2024)

detail.title: Industrial Policy as Market-Shaping Competition: Evidence from China, the European Union, and the United States (2009-2024)
detail.abstract: This paper documents the evolution of contemporary industrial policy across China, the European Union, and the United States between 2009 and 2024 using an extended panel from the New Industrial Policy Observatory. Focusing on selective industrial actions that plausibly alter relative competitive conditions, the analysis characterises industrial policy as a persistent, market-shaping phenomenon rather than a temporary response to macroeconomic shocks. Ten stylised facts document a sharp and sustained expansion in industrial policy activity after 2019, a reorientation of stated policy motives toward security and resilience and increasing concentration of interventions in strategic and dual-use sectors. Industrial actions increasingly propagate across jurisdictions through rapid crosscountry sequencing. Subsidies diffuse quickly among major economies and are frequently followed by import restrictions in large domestic markets, while defensive trade measures become more rival-directed. At the same time, policy instruments diverge in persistence: export restrictions have become structurally durable, whereas import barriers remain more contingent. Taken together, the evidence points to a shift from episodic intervention toward a competitive and sequential industrial policy regime organised around strategic value chains and chokepoints, with important implications for trade governance and the multilateral trading system.

title: Brief of 76 Scholars of Law, Business, Economics, and Medicine as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners, Hikma Pharmaceuticals v. Amarin Pharma, Inc. et al.
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers Law School, American University Washington College of Law, West Virginia University - College of Law and Harvard University - Harvard Medical School

detail.title: Brief of 76 Scholars of Law, Business, Economics, and Medicine as Amici Curiae in Support of Petitioners, Hikma Pharmaceuticals v. Amarin Pharma, Inc. et al.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
For a century and a half, the doctrine of inducement of patent infringement has required an act that is specific, unambiguous, and affirmative. Conduct that (1) does not specifically encourage infringement, (2) is ambiguous as to infringing or noninfringing behavior, or (3) is an omission has long been insufficient for patent inducement liability.

In Hikma v. Amarin, the Federal Circuit disregarded these principles. The court held that inducement liability could arise based on speculative inferences from general marketing statements and mandatory drug labeling text--statements that bore no specificity to the patented methods of use at issue. That holding followed the court's 2021 decision in GlaxoSmithKline LLC v. Teva Pharmaceuticals USA, which also expanded patent inducement beyond its historic bounds.

Such expansion is not just wrong on the law--it threatens the statutory scheme for generic drug competition, the innovation economy, the patent system's foundational principles, and patient health and welfare. This brief, submitted on behalf of 76 professors of law, business, economics, and medicine, argues that the Supreme Court should return inducement law to its well-established roots.

title: Urban Infoanalytics: Bridging the Gap between City Data and Governance A Framework for Effective Decision Infrastructure

detail.title: Urban Infoanalytics: Bridging the Gap between City Data and Governance A Framework for Effective Decision Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
Cities today have never been technically 'smarter'; we have sensors, satellites, and advanced models for almost everything. Yet, the actual work of running a city often feels as slow and reactive as ever. The problem isn’t that we lack data; it’s that this data rarely connects with the people who need to make decisions in the moment.

This paper introduces Urban Infoanalytics, a methodology designed to bridge that disconnected 'last mile' between raw numbers and real institutional action. Instead of just generating more complex data, we propose flipping the workflow: starting with the decision that needs to be made and working backward. The key is embedding 'Translators', staff fluent in both policy and code, directly into municipal teams. This turns static dashboards into an active decision infrastructure. Ultimately, success isn't about the perfection of the model; it is about whether the city runs faster, responds better, and allocates resources more fairly.

title: The Adoption of Quantum Computing Technologies
affiliations: ETH Zürich and Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: The Adoption of Quantum Computing Technologies
detail.abstract: Quantum computing can revolutionize search methods by boosting their cost efficiency. In this paper we analyze under which conditions companies should adopt quantum computing for search problems, by considering the core functioning of quantum search algorithms. Whereas classical search allows incremental discovery-firms learn immediately whether a candidate solution is valid-a quantum search algorithm must inspect all candidates in superposition and can reveal results only after the inspection of all elements is completed. We show that this difference in timing of information revelation fundamentally alters the competitive outcome. In monopoly settings, quantum search provides the expected cost efficiency. Under competition, however, delayed revelation eliminates the economic speedup: when the number of competitors is large, classical search dominates quantum search despite its higher computational cost when there is a premium for early discovery. Quantum adoption becomes optimal only for sufficiently complex problems where search-cost efficiency outweighs the early discovery premium. These results highlight that a quantum speedup does not automatically translate into economic advantage and provide conditions under which firms should adopt quantum search technologies.

title: Intelligence as Trajectory-Dominant Pareto Optimization
affiliations: Clevix AI Research and Clevix LLC

detail.title: Intelligence as Trajectory-Dominant Pareto Optimization
detail.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence have produced systems with impressive task-level performance, yet many display an early saturation in long-horizon adaptability despite continued optimization. Standard evaluation paradigms-centered on point-wise performance, terminal outcomes, or static multi-objective trade-offs-struggle to explain why systems that remain locally optimal nevertheless become developmentally constrained over time. In this work, we argue that this limitation arises from a deeper mischaracterization of intelligence itself. We propose a foundational reformulation in which intelligence is understood as a property of agent trajectories rather than isolated states. Within this view, we introduce trajectorydominant Pareto optimization, a path-wise generalization of classical Pareto optimality where dominance relations are defined over accumulated multi-objective costs along entire trajectories. This formulation reveals the existence of Pareto traps: regions of trajectory space that are locally nondominated yet globally restrictive, preventing access to alternative developmental paths without temporary degradation. To clarify the structure of these constraints, we develop a mathematical taxonomy of Pareto traps based on their geometric signatures, and introduce the Trap Escape Difficulty Index (TEDI), an intrinsic measure of how difficult it is for an agent to escape a given trap. Dynamic intelligence ceilings emerge naturally as geometric consequences of trajectory-level dominance, with TEDI providing a principled way to compare the rigidity of such ceilings across systems and optimization regimes. We illustrate these ideas using a minimal model contrasting point-wise and trajectory-dominant agents, showing how ceiling formation and escape arise independently of architectural limits or computational scale. By shifting attention from local performance to trajectory accessibility, this framework offers a structural explanation for longhorizon stagnation and establishes a foundation for studying adaptive restructuring, developmental phase transitions, and commitment-aware intelligent systems.

title: NEXAT: A System-Based Approach to Integrated and Soil-Conserving Crop Production

detail.title: NEXAT: A System-Based Approach to Integrated and Soil-Conserving Crop Production

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests or financial relationships that could have influenced the outcomes of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study as it does not involve human or animal subjects. All data were obtained from publicly available sources or manufacturer documentation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted without external funding.

detail.abstract: Agricultural mechanization over the past century has largely evolved through incremental optimization of specialized machines, resulting in fragmented field operations, high energy consumption, repeated soil compaction, and increasing capital intensity. NEXAT (Next Generation Agriculture Technology) represents a fundamentally different approach by rethinking crop production as a unified technical system rather than a collection of independent machines. Developed by NEXAT GmbH in Germany, the NEXAT concept integrates all major arable farming operations including tillage, seeding, fertilization, crop protection, and harvesting into a single modular carrier platform operating under a wide-span controlled traffic farming framework. This paper presents a system-level analysis of the NEXAT concept, focusing on its technical architecture, operational principles, agronomic rationale, economic positioning, and sustainability claims. The study critically evaluates the potential of NEXAT to reduce soil compaction, improve operational efficiency, and enable regenerative farming practices, while also identifying structural limitations, adoption barriers, and research gaps.

title: A Field Experiment on the Effectiveness of Framing Climate Action: Direct vs. Indirect Effects
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, ESSEC Business School, Geneva Finance Research Institute, University of Alberta and York University - Schulich School of Business

detail.title: A Field Experiment on the Effectiveness of Framing Climate Action: Direct vs. Indirect Effects

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study protocol was approved by the research ethics committee of Montpellier Business School.

detail.abstract:
Climate action remains insufficient to meet Paris Agreement targets, creating an urgent need to understand how to effectively motivate individual pro-environmental behavior. While traditional approaches emphasize the direct impact of individual behavioral changes, we investigate whether highlighting the indirect effects of social contagion—where one's behavior influences others—can more effectively drive climate action.

Through a field experiment with 579 business school students participating in Climate Collage workshops, we compare two message framings: a "direct effect" approach emphasizing personal carbon footprint reduction, and an "indirect effect" approach emphasizing how visible behavior changes can influence others and create new social norms. We measure both pro-environmental behaviors (PEBs) and behavioral visibility (sharing behaviors on social media and with others).

Our findings reveal that while both framings equally increase PEBs, the indirect framing significantly increases participants' sharing of environmental behaviors on social media three weeks post-intervention. Importantly, this effect is moderated by individual psychological traits: the indirect framing is most effective for individuals high in negative environmental outcome affect and low in resistance to coercion. Post-hoc analysis shows that indirect framing better alleviates negative emotions elicited by climate education.

These findings contribute to institutional theory's microfoundations by demonstrating that awareness of one's role as an influencer can motivate behavior change, though message tailoring based on individual traits is critical. Our results offer practical insights for designing high-impact climate education interventions that leverage social contagion effects.

title: Tariff Changes in the U.S. from 1840-2024: A Narrative Analysis
affiliations: Northwestern University and

detail.title: Tariff Changes in the U.S. from 1840-2024: A Narrative Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper contains a detailed narrative analysis of legislative tariff changes in the United States from 1840-2024. The primary aim of this account is to provide the basis for the classification of tariff changes used in den Besten and Känzig (2025), which in turn allows for the identification of the causal effects of tariff policy on the economy. We systematically identify major tariff policy changes, place each reform in its economic and political context, and assess the stated motivations based on contemporary narrative sources. In this way, we distinguish between tariff changes driven by plausibly exogenous considerations and those responding to prevailing economic conditions. Our narrative analysis identifies 35 major tariff reforms between 1840 and the present. Of these, we classify 21 tariff changes as exogenous and 14 as endogenous. We also hope the narrative account, historiographical research and data contained in this paper is interesting in its own right. To our knowledge, no existing study provides a systematic analysis of the motives behind U.S. tariff policy over such a long historical horizon, spanning from the mid-19th century to the modern era.

title: Education - The Key to the Success of the New Zimbabwean Currency (ZWG)
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Education - The Key to the Success of the New Zimbabwean Currency (ZWG)
detail.abstract: Money has been evolving since the advent of civilisation, with people exchanging goods (barter trade) in the early years. Later, precious stones were used to pay for goods and services, and in recent years, the use of crypto assets has been on the rise. In 2021, El Salvador became the first country to adopt Bitcoin as a legal tender, and the government has recently identified the need to provide Bitcoin education to the citizens. Recently, the Zimbabwean government introduced a structured currency in an attempt to stabilise the economy through the curbing of excessive inflation, among other measures. Similar to El Salvador's investment in Bitcoin education, it is critical for the Zimbabwean government to invest in the education of its citizens regarding the new structured currency. Thus, the aim of this paper is to raise the awareness of Zimbabwean citizens, by critically interrogating the viability of the new structured currency. To achieve the above, an exploratory study, in form of literature review was used. From the results obtained, it was found that the value of the Zimbabwean structured currency is influenced by the following factors; gold reserves, gold prices, economic indicators, government policies, market demand of the currency, global events, trust and confidence, political differences, multi-currency system, informal sector activities, availability of foreign currency, speculation and market sentiment, and exchange rates. Furthermore, these factors were divided into three categories namely; primary factors, secondary factors, and tertiary factors. In conclusion, it was determined that the new Zimbabwean structured currency is a viable enabler to Zimbabwe's 2030 development goals.

title: Russia's Money Cliff: Paying for War After Petrodollars Vanish
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Russia's Money Cliff: Paying for War After Petrodollars Vanish
detail.abstract: Russia's war in Ukraine isn't just a military problem-it's also becoming a liquidity problem. Moscow burns roughly $200 million a day. When oil buyers pay less or fewer barrels flow due to attacks and ship seizures, the Kremlin will have to start selling the country itself. Russia holds about $350 billion of gold, its most truly liquid asset. In its National Wealth Fund, Moscow holds approximately $100 billion worth of Chinese RMB, Sberbank shares, and other "accessible" foreign exchange. In a crisis, these assets wouldn't fetch full value. The RMB isn't freely convertible and Sberbank shares are illiquid. A $50B recovery value is probably generous. Each billion USD could realistically fund 3-to-4 days of warfare at today's intensity.

title: On the Asymmetry Between Conflict and Development: Evidence from Sustainable Development Goals
affiliations: Center for Natural Resource Studies (CNRS) and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: On the Asymmetry Between Conflict and Development: Evidence from Sustainable Development Goals
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between (internal) armed conflict and sustainable development. Using annual panel data on 192 countries from 2000 to 2024, we employ a variety of econometric techniques to trace the impulse responses between conflict fatalities and Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) performance in both directions. Results reveal a striking asymmetry: conflict shocks produce long-lasting adverse effects on SDG performance, while SDG performance shocks exert only transient effects on conflict intensity. This asymmetry persists across external and major conflict episodes, and is robust to alternative identification strategies. Our findings indicate that sustainable development is fundamentally contingent on prior achievement of peace.

title: Cultural Adaptation and the Uneven Emergence of Large-Scale Cooperation
affiliations: Brown University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Cultural Adaptation and the Uneven Emergence of Large-Scale Cooperation
detail.abstract: This essay suggests that the evolution of human cooperation over the course of human history should be viewed as a two-layer process. A foundational layer, rooted in subsistence and ecological pressures, shaped cooperative dispositions unevenly, whereas an expansionary layer, rooted in conflict and stratification, generated large-scale cooperation in societies in which its seeds were formed. The first evolutionary layer unfolded over the grand arc of human evolution, reinforcing the capacity for small-scale cooperation in hunter-gatherer societies while favoring traits complementary to cooperation only in some sedentary societies. The second evolutionary layer emerged as rising population density heightened external threats, fostered coercive centralized authority, and raised the returns to public infrastructure. In environments where cooperative traits had already evolved, warfare, extraction, and infrastructure provision reinforced these predispositions, transforming them into durable collective institutions. Yet in settings where such cultural foundations were absent, large-scale collective action was more challenging, and conflict was often destabilizing, magnifying division and political fragility. Recognizing the profound global heterogeneity in this foundational layer of cooperative behavior is essential for identifying the origins of large-scale cooperation and the conditions under which conflict reinforced cooperative capacity rather than intensifying fragmentation.

title: Industrial Policy in the Global Semiconductor Sector
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, University of British Columbia (UBC), affiliation not provided to SSRN, , and

detail.title: Industrial Policy in the Global Semiconductor Sector
detail.abstract: The resurgence of subsidies and industrial policies has raised concerns about their potential inefficiency and alignment with multilateral principles. Critics warn that such policies may divert resources to less efficient firms and provoke retaliatory measures from other countries, leading to a wasteful “subsidy race.” However, subsidies for sectors with inherent cross-border externalities can have positive global effects. This paper examines these issues within the semiconductor industry: a key driver of economic growth and innovation with potentially significant learning-by-doing and strategic importance due to its dual-use applications. Our study aims to: (1) document and quantify recent industrial policies in the global semiconductor sector, (2) explore the rationale behind these policies, and (3) evaluate their economic impacts, particularly their cross-border effects, and compatibility with multilateral principles. We employ historical analysis, natural language processing, and a model-based approach to measure government support and its impacts. Our findings indicate that government support has been vital for the industry’s growth, with subsidies being the primary form of support. They also highlight the importance of cross-border technology transfers through FDI, business and research collaborations, and technology licensing. China, despite significant subsidies, does not stand out as an outlier compared to other countries, given its market size. Model estimates suggest the presence of learning-by-doing at the firm-product level as well as economies of scope within a firm and substantial cross-border learning spillovers. These spillovers likely reflect cross-country technology transfers and the role of fabless clients and input suppliers in disseminating knowledge globally through their interactions with foundries. Such cross-border spillovers are not merely accidental but result from deliberate actions by market participants that cannot be taken for granted. Firms may choose to share knowledge across borders or restrict access to frontier technology, thereby excluding certain countries. Future research will use model estimates to simulate the quantitative implications of subsidies and to explore the dynamics of a “subsidy race” in the semiconductor industry.

title: The Invisible Firm
affiliations: Indiana University Maurer School of Law and Indiana University Maurer School of Law

detail.title: The Invisible Firm

publicationDetails.detailsText: Indiana Legal Studies Research Paper No. 571
publicationDetails.journalName: Indiana University Maurer School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Family offices are the most powerful institutions you have never heard of. They are largely unknown for three reasons. First, they defy easy characterization. Second, they occupy a rare space that is only available to ultrahigh-net-worth individuals. And third, quietly managing trillions in private wealth, these entities operate beyond the reach of most financial regulation. Yet, they have a hand in reshaping the architecture of global capital. 

This Article offers the first comprehensive legal and economic account of the emergence of the modern family office. Drawing on foundational work in transaction cost economics, agency theory, and public choice, it explains how family offices minimize costs, preserve privacy, and exploit regulatory carveouts like the Family Office Rule. In doing so, this Article demonstrates that family offices represent a rational, equilibrium response to legal incentives--what Ronald Coase might call the "firm made private." In this way, family offices produce efficiencies and yield positive externalities that make them valuable not only to their principals but to society. 

Yet, as family offices proliferate, critics warn that their opacity, wealth-concentrating power, and potential for abuse pose growing systemic risks. This Article critically evaluates these concerns, assessing whether family offices are engines of inequality, vectors of financial instability, or surprisingly efficient vehicles for private ordering. We find greater support for the argument that family offices are exceptional private-ordering, if wealth-maximizing, vehicles that produce more benefit than harm.

title: Sports Betting Across Borders: Spatial Spillovers, Credit Distress, and Fiscal Externalities
affiliations: and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Sports Betting Across Borders: Spatial Spillovers, Credit Distress, and Fiscal Externalities

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1184
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Since the 2018 Murphy v. NCAA decision, 38 states have legalized mobile sports betting. We study effects on betting and consumer credit, emphasizing spatial spillovers across state lines. Using consumer spending data and an extended two-way fixed effects framework that separately identifies direct and spillover effects, we find that legalization increases total sportsbook spending roughly tenfold and take-up by 3.1 percentage points. Counties in non-legal states within 15 miles of a legal state experience spillover spending equal to roughly 14 percent of the direct effect, with these spillovers declining to roughly zero by 60 miles. Using the New York Fed Consumer Credit Panel, we find that median credit scores decline by roughly 1 point and overall delinquency rises 0.3 percentage points from a 10.7 percent base, with spillover delinquency rising nearly 0.2 percentage points. Under-40 auto loan delinquency increases by half a percentage point and credit card delinquency by one percentage point, driving the overall increase in delinquency. Scaling the population-level delinquency effect by take-up yields implied delinquency increases of roughly 10 percentage points among induced bettors. We conclude with a policy simulation which reveals that spillovers create a fiscal asymmetry: states that have not legalized bear costs from cross-border betting without capturing tax revenue, giving high exposure states a stronger case for legalization. This incentive is increasing in states that have higher pre-legalization betting activity, population centers near legal states, and a younger population. Methodologically, we show that ignoring spatial spillovers can contribute to attenuated estimates and an under-count of the affected population.

title: Clauses To Look Out For: A Legal Guide For Foundries
affiliations: Advocate, Kolkata, India

detail.title: Clauses To Look Out For: A Legal Guide For Foundries
detail.abstract:
Foundries operate in a high-risk commercial environment where contract terms often determine profitability more than manufacturing efficiency. In the last few years, Indian foundries have become increasingly integrated into global supply chains. However, the global economy has grown more volatile due to geopolitical tensions, evolving trade policy, and supply chain disruptions. In this environment, contracts are not merely legal documents they are risk allocation tools, which should consider the following: a) high level of competition and rapid technological change; b) changes in anticipated government incentives; c) disruptions, delays, trade tensions, or shortages; d) evolving regulatory and legal requirements across many jurisdictions; e) geopolitical and international trade conditions; f) impacts of the COVID-19 or similar such pandemic; and g) other risks and uncertainties. 

Foundry businesses must now contend with a parallel external development: renewed uncertainty in global trade relationships, including recent tariff-related friction between India and the United States. For export-oriented engineering suppliers, this adds a layer of commercial unpredictability that cannot be addressed through policy announcements alone. 

In this context, the foundry sector's resilience in 2026 will depend not only on production capability, but also on contract strength and risk allocation discipline. This article highlights the key clauses foundries must negotiate or look out for and provides a contract playbook tailored for foundry management teams.

title: Open-Ended Treasury Purchases: From Market Functioning to Financial Easing
affiliations: , , Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas and Northwestern University

detail.title: Open-Ended Treasury Purchases: From Market Functioning to Financial Easing

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1183
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We assess whether the Fed's asset purchases can be tailored to either restore market functioning or provide economic stimulus. When the communicated goal is restoring market functioning and purchases' implementation is flexible, flow effects are significant: relative price deviations narrow. However, stock effects remain near zero and hence not stimulative. When the communicated goal links purchases to the achievement of the dual mandate, improving their size's predictability, stock effects rise consistently above zero. When the communicated implementation improves the predictability of the purchases' maturity composition, stock effects become large. Jointly, the communicated goal and implementation can shape the purchases' effects.

title: RBI Draft Registration Amendment Directions 2026: A Move Toward Proportionate NBFC Regulation-With Caveats
affiliations: Advocate, Kolkata, India

detail.title: RBI Draft Registration Amendment Directions 2026: A Move Toward Proportionate NBFC Regulation-With Caveats
detail.abstract:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued the Draft Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Registration, Exemptions and Framework for Scale Based Regulation) Amendment Directions, 2026(“Draft Directions”), inviting public comments by March 4, 2026.

The draft proposes a targeted recalibration of the NBFC regulatory framework, particularly for smaller, low-risk entities, by introducing a pathway for exemption from registration for select NBFCs. While the policy direction is clearly aligned with risk-based and proportional regulation, certain accompanying clarifications (FAQs) may require refinement to ensure that the intended relief is not diluted in practice. This paper discusses the further refinements required.

title: Trading on History: Similarity-Based Analogical Reasoning in Futures Markets

detail.title: Trading on History: Similarity-Based Analogical Reasoning in Futures Markets
detail.abstract: From the perspective of economic theory, trading activities by non-institutional investors are fundamentally driven by utility maximization. Distinct from the hedging mandates of institutional entities, individual agents participate in capital markets primarily to generate capital gains, thereby facilitating wealth accumulation and the smoothing of intertemporal consumption. This article presents a synoptic review of the study by Chiang, Chiu, and Kuo (2021), originally published in the Pacific-Basin Finance Journal. Drawing upon an exclusive interview with co-author Professor Wei-Yu Kuo (Department of International Business, National Chengchi University), this paper elucidates the theoretical underpinnings and empirical validity of Similarity-Based Trading Rules (SBTR). This article is published in the NCCU Business Review (See: https://nccubr.nccu.edu.tw/articles/16).

title: Intergenerational Spillovers of Environmental Attitudes and Behaviors
affiliations: , Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, Northeastern University (USA), Northeastern University (USA), World Bank,  and Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance

detail.title: Intergenerational Spillovers of Environmental Attitudes and Behaviors
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether environmental education can shift household behavior through intergenerational transmission of knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes. We implement an activity-based program in Patna, India, and conduct a randomized experiment with 1,545 child–parent pairs assigned to child-only, parent-only, joint, or control groups. Direct participation increases pro-environmental behaviors. Spillovers occur but are asymmetric: while children and parents influence each other’s behaviors, only children significantly shift parents’ climate beliefs and attitudes. Joint participation yields no additional gains beyond individual participation, suggesting that targeting children alone may be a scalable and cost-effective strategy for promoting sustainable household practices.

title: Monotonicity, Escalation, and Admissibility in Scoring Rules
affiliations: Merope

detail.title: Monotonicity, Escalation, and Admissibility in Scoring Rules
detail.abstract: Numerical evaluation systems commonly rely on monotone aggregation rules to combine scores submitted by multiple evaluators. While monotonicity is widely viewed as a minimal coherence requirement, this paper shows that, on unrestricted or weakly restricted reporting domains, monotone aggregation generically generates escalation incentives whenever evaluators retain influence for arbitrarily extreme reporting profiles. In such environments, bounded optimal reports may fail to exist, rendering incentive analysis ill posed independently of strategic interaction or equilibrium considerations. The paper identifies eventual loss of influence as a minimal structural condition for stabilising incentives under monotone aggregation. It introduces evaluator-level admissibility, a screening mechanism that conditions whether an evaluator's entire reporting profile influences the aggregate outcome based on its deviation from a consensus benchmark scaled by dispersion. Admissibility operates at the level of evaluators rather than individual scores: evaluators assess candidates, while the mechanism evaluates evaluators. Conditional on retained influence, aggregation remains fully monotone and unchanged. Three main results are established. First, escalation is unavoidable under monotone aggregation whenever influence persists for arbitrarily extreme reports in environments where retained influence can dominate loss of influence. Second, evaluator-level admissibility is sufficient to bound escalation endogenously, without imposing ex ante domain restrictions or hard reporting caps. Third, attenuation of influence alone is insufficient: some form of eventual loss of influence is necessary to stabilise incentives. By shifting the unit of analysis from scores to evaluator reporting profiles, the paper provides a structural explanation for the stabilising role of evaluator-level screening mechanisms in numerical evaluation systems.

title: Set-Identified SDEs for Quantitative Finance: Robust Drift Bounds, Girsanov Stability, and No-Arbitrage Pricing Intervals

detail.title: Set-Identified SDEs for Quantitative Finance: Robust Drift Bounds, Girsanov Stability, and No-Arbitrage Pricing Intervals
detail.abstract: We study continuous-time asset models where the diffusion is observable up to estimation error, but the drift is only partially identified from discrete data and market microstructure noise. Rather than committing to a single parametric specification, we model the drift as belonging to a convex uncertainty set and derive (i) explicit bounds on attainable equivalent martingale measures, (ii) stability guarantees for likelihood ratios under drift perturbations via Girsanov theory, and (iii) no-arbitrage pricing intervals for contingent claims under drift ambiguity. Our results provide a mathematically transparent link between statistical non-identification and robust pricing, yielding tractable confidence regions for risk premia and option values.

title: When Antitrust and the First Amendment Collide
affiliations: Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies

detail.title: When Antitrust and the First Amendment Collide
detail.abstract:
This essay examines the clash between antitrust enforcement and First Amendment protections when addressing alleged “Big Tech censorship.” The essay focuses on then-FTC Commissioner (now Chair) Andrew Ferguson’s concurrence in FTC v. 1661, Inc. d/b/a GOAT (December 2024) where Ferguson urges vigorous enforcement against platforms limiting free speech, targeting (1) alleged collusion on content moderation policies (citing Murthy v. Missouri) and (2) advertiser boycotts as illegal concerted refusals to deal.  Ferguson cites the post-Musk advertiser exodus from X (facilitated by GARM, which disbanded amid scrutiny) and NewsGuard’s ratings system as examples harming conservative-leaning platforms.

This essay argues that Ferguson’s approach is legally problematic. Antitrust laws target economic restraints in trade or commerce, not private speech regulation—misapplying them risks exceeding statutory authority and lacking proof of economic harm.  Ferguson’s collusion claims also contradict Murthy’s record, which found platforms acted under government coercion, not conspiracy. Supreme Court precedents like Moody v. NetChoice (2024) affirm platforms’ First Amendment editorial rights and warn against government-forced speech changes.  On boycotts, while anticompetitive collusion to exclude rivals violates antitrust (e.g., FTC v. Superior Court Trial Lawyers Ass’n), ideologically motivated refusals to deal are protected expression (NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware), with no general duty to deal (FTC v. Qualcomm).  Forcing dealings based on distasteful speech raises serious First Amendment issues (see, e.g., Manhattan Community Access Corp. v. Halleck; 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis).  Spiwak warns Ferguson’s threats echo Biden-era jawboning and risk due process violations, similar to former Chair Lina Khan’s overreach.  Spiwak urges focusing on statutory bounds to restore the FTC’s bipartisan reputation, emphasizing that antitrust cannot override constitutional tolerance for diverse speech.

title: Granular Portfolios, Expectations, and International Capital Flows
affiliations: University of Lausanne - School of Economics and Business Administration (HEC-Lausanne), Swiss Federal Finance Administration and King’s College London

detail.title: Granular Portfolios, Expectations, and International Capital Flows

declarations.funderStatement: The authors acknowledge financial support from the Swiss National Foundation grant number 100018_219537.

detail.abstract: We identify a novel channel of international financial contagion driven by investor expectations. Using a unique dataset linking investors' cross-country GDP growth expectations to their equity mutual fund investments and to funds' country allocations, we show that inflows into mutual funds respond strongly to fund-level expected growth, whereas funds' country allocations react only weakly to country-specific expectations. This asymmetry generates co-ownership spillovers: negative expectations about one country propagate mechanically to other countries held in the same funds, even in the absence of changes in the country's own expected fundamentals. We develop a portfolio choice model with delegated investment and portfolio stickiness to rationalize this pattern. Because country weights in global portfolios are highly granular, these spillovers are quantitatively important, accounting for about 80% of expectation-driven capital flow reallocation. Small countries are disproportionately exposed to these spillovers, while large countries are their main sources.

title: GAST-DRO: Generalised Adversarial Stress Testing with Distributionally Robust Optimisation for UK SME Credit Portfolios

detail.title: GAST-DRO: Generalised Adversarial Stress Testing with Distributionally Robust Optimisation for UK SME Credit Portfolios

detail.abstract: Stress testing and portfolio optimisation for SME lending remain challenging because losses are driven by a small number of highly correlated, fat-tailed events. This paper introduces GAST-DRO (Generalised Adversarial Stress Testing with Distributionally Robust Optimisation), a scenario-based framework that (i) generates correlated macro-sector stress scenarios augmented with adversarial 'worst-plausible' stresses, and (ii) chooses credit allocations that are robust to distributional uncertainty by penalising the dispersion of scenario losses. Using a synthetic UK SME loan portfolio of 100,000 facilities (£31.5bn exposure) and a stratified 10,000-borrower sample for tractable optimisation, we compare GAST-DRO to a sample-average (risk-neutral) optimiser, a Basel-style heuristic haircut, an equal-weight baseline, a classical mean-variance optimiser, and a CVaR optimiser. Across held-out stress scenarios, GAST-DRO reduces 99% Value-at-Risk and expected loss by approximately 24% relative to sample-average optimisation, while increasing Basel IRB-style RWA density by only 0.16 percentage points. Backtesting on three calibrated historical crises (GFC 2008-09, COVID-19 2020, and the Eurozone debt crisis 2011-12) indicates consistent tail-risk improvements and material portfolio-level savings when scaled to the full exposure. Sensitivity and bootstrap analyses suggest the tail-risk gains are robust to the ambiguity radius once ε exceeds a small threshold.

title: Azerbaijan's Economy In 2026: New Perspectives of the New Order
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Azerbaijan's Economy In 2026: New Perspectives of the New Order
detail.abstract: This research evaluates the risks and challenges of Azerbaijan's socioeconomic development during the 2026 reporting year, within the geopolitical context of the Venezuelan political crisis and other potential events (such as the Russia-Ukraine war, Israel-Iran confrontation, and US-China trade tensions) amid oil price volatility. According to international sources (IEA Oil 2025, EIA), oil prices are expected to stabilize within the $51-66 range in 2026 due to oversupply, though short-term risks may cause temporary increases. For instance, while an increase in Venezuela's daily oil production from 1 million to 2 million barrels could impact prices, it is anticipated that Venezuela will not have a significant market impact this year due to limited technological, financial, and time-related constraints regarding production expansion. In this context, to ensure the sustainability of socioeconomic development, Azerbaijan must focus on economic diversification and replacing oil revenues with alternative income sources.

title: Murthy Provides a Teachable Moment about the "Vast Power" of the Administrative State
affiliations: Phoenix Center for Advanced Legal & Economic Public Policy Studies

detail.title: Murthy Provides a Teachable Moment about the "Vast Power" of the Administrative State
detail.abstract:
This essay examines the Supreme Court’s ruling in Murthy v. Missouri (2024) to highlight the dangers of government jawboning on private speech and the overwhelming influence of the administrative state.  In Murthy, petitioners alleged Biden Administration coercion turned platforms into state actors by pressuring them to suppress COVID-19 misinformation.  Despite a “sprawling” record of threats—including antitrust actions, regulatory reforms, and Section 230 changes—the Court dismissed for lack of standing, deeming injuries insufficiently “concrete and particularized.”  This decision contrasts with the Court’s unanimous decision in NRA v. Vullo (2024), where direct government pressure on insurers granted the NRA standing, prohibiting coercion to suppress disfavored views.

This essay probes the central puzzle: why didn’t the platforms sue, given likely success under Vullo?  One can probably attributes this decision to the administrative state’s “vast power,” as Chief Justice Roberts described, encompassing ex ante regulation (e.g., taxes, securities), ex post enforcement (e.g., antitrust by DOJ/FTC), and subsidies from laws like the American Rescue Plan (2021), Inflation Reduction Act (2022), and CHIPS Act (2022).  In other words, it is just too hard to fight City Hall.  The problem, however, is that this regulatory asymmetry fosters bilateral bargaining between the regulator and the regulated, where firms acquiesce to informal demands by the government to avoid retaliation, yielding unpredictable, non-transparent policy outcomes detached from legal precedent.

title: Arrival Inequality in International Tourism Cities: A Matthew Effect in Global Growth

detail.title: Arrival Inequality in International Tourism Cities: A Matthew Effect in Global Growth
detail.abstract: This study empirically tests the Matthew Effect hypothesis in global urban tourism, examining whether initial advantage leads to disproportionate growth among the world's top 100 city destinations (2017-2019). Using a mixed-methods framework, we analysed international arrivals and attraction infrastructure in the top 10, employing Gini coefficients and Palma ratios to assess inequality. The study reveals moderate, structural inequality (Gini = 0.369) rather than cumulative advantage. Tier-based factors (92.1%) dominated regional factors (8.7%) in explaining inequality. Contrary to the Matthew Effect, larger cities showed slower growth, demonstrating convergence. We found significant gaps between attraction infrastructure and arrival rankings (e.g., Istanbul #10 arrivals, #2 quality; Hong Kong #1 arrivals, #9 quality). These findings challenge the Matthew Effect in tourism, suggesting inequality stems from structural segmentation. Mid-tier destinations can compete via strategic investment, as flows are driven by brand and positioning, not just infrastructure. The results suggest more equitable development opportunities exist. This is the first comprehensive empirical test of this hypothesis in urban tourism and is limited to pre-pandemic data.

title: Innovation-induced Bank Runs: Run in and Run out
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Institute of Economics, Tsinghua University and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Innovation-induced Bank Runs: Run in and Run out
detail.abstract: This paper examines how competition for scarce innovative projects can lead to premature adoption of financial innovations and increase systemic risk. We develop a model in which financial institutions (FIs) compete to finance a limited pool of new projects whose failure rate is uncertain. The rivalry for market share creates a preemptive motive that distorts incentives for patient learning, leading to inefficiently early entry (“run in”) and heightened vulnerability to bank runs (“run in”). By embedding uncertainty and endogenous learning into a Diamond-Dybvig framework, we show that decentralized competition results in excessive early investment, reduced screening effort, and a higher probability of bank runs compared to a monopolistic or socially planned allocation. Our analysis suggests that monopolistic ownership or intellectual property protection could mitigate these inefficiencies and reduce social hazards.

title: Economic Consequences Across Generations: How Parental Health Shocks Affect Adult Children's Fertility in China
affiliations: Wuhan University, Cardiff University Business School and Zhongnan University of Economics and Law

detail.title: Economic Consequences Across Generations: How Parental Health Shocks Affect Adult Children's Fertility in China
detail.abstract: Parental health shocks are associated with the fertility choices of adult children in China. Using a comprehensive longitudinal dataset of Chinese households, it traces parental diagnoses of major illnesses in early stages to delayed childbirth and fewer births among adult offspring., We employ two matching methodologies: Coarsened Exact Matching (CEM) and Propensity Score Matching (PSM). Our estimates indicate that parental health shocks are associated with a 10.5% lower probability of having (an additional) child and significantly postpone the timing of first, second, and third births for both sons and daughters. The magnitude of these associations is larger among low-income households, families without medical insurance, and those in the non-public sector, and when adult children co-reside with their parents. Through economic channels—specifically, increased caregiving burdens and financial constraints—parental health shocks create resource reallocation within families that affects fertility timing and quantity. This paper quantifies the economic implications of parental health shocks for fertility behavior in a low-social security environment.

title: Perceptions of Trauma-Informed Competencies Among Clinical Social Workers: Practice Implications for Assessment, Training, and Workforce Development

detail.title: Perceptions of Trauma-Informed Competencies Among Clinical Social Workers: Practice Implications for Assessment, Training, and Workforce Development

declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is based on qualitative data derived from doctoral research. All procedures involving human participants were conducted in accordance with applicable ethical standards, including informed consent and confidentiality protections. Data were collected and analyzed in de-identified form for scholarly purposes.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Trauma-informed practice is widely recognized as foundational in clinical social work, yet less is known about how clinicians perceive their preparedness to assess and respond to trauma in realworld practice settings. This exploratory qualitative study examined licensed clinical social workers' perceptions of trauma-informed competencies, with particular attention to assessment practices, training pathways, and workforce development experiences. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine licensed clinical social workers providing direct clinical services across diverse practice settings. Data were analyzed using Wolcott's three-phase qualitative analytic approach, supported by reflexive memoing, an audit trail, and thick description to enhance trustworthiness. Three themes emerged: (1) trauma-related preparedness developed unevenly and was frequently acquired post-degree; (2) clinicians relied primarily on general clinical skills and broad mental health screening tools rather than trauma-specific assessments; and (3) knowledge of trauma-specific assessment instruments varied widely and was closely tied to access to continuing education and organizational support. Findings suggest that trauma-informed competence in practice is shaped less by standardized graduate preparation and more by postgraduate training opportunities and agency context. Implications are discussed for clinical practice, supervision, workforce development, and continuing education.

title:
Liquidity vs. Value Retention 

LVD Model: Dualistic State-Based Decision Model for Institutional Real Estate Investments / New Allocation Theory and Portfolio Strategy Models

detail.title:
Liquidity vs. Value Retention 

LVD Model: Dualistic State-Based Decision Model for Institutional Real Estate Investments / New Allocation Theory and Portfolio Strategy Models
detail.abstract: This thesis introduces the Liquidity-Value-Duration (LVD) model, a state-based decision framework for institutional real estate investments. The model addresses a central limitation of standard valuation and portfolio methods, which treat liquidity and long-term value as a single objective despite their different economic roles in illiquid assets. In the LVD framework, liquidity is modeled as a time- and state-dependent constraint that limits the realizability of returns. Value efficiency is defined through stable cash flows, capital efficiency, and long-term value preservation under uncertainty. Interest rate volatility, regime changes, and correlation effects are explicitly incorporated to reflect changing macro-financial conditions. The model combines methods from financial economics, decision theory, and real estate economics. Investment choices are not derived from the maximization of a single metric but are evaluated within a two-dimensional efficiency space. This allows for clear, state-dependent trade-offs between liquidity-oriented and value-oriented strategies. The contribution of the model lies in its ability to explain persistent allocation patterns observed in institutional real estate portfolios. The framework abstracts from detailed market microstructure and relies on simplified state dynamics, which limits short-term precision but supports structural clarity and future empirical extension.

title: Iran: A Nation on Edge

title: Benchmarking Private Credit
affiliations: Aalto University School of Business and Aalto University School of Business

detail.title: Benchmarking Private Credit
detail.abstract: We provide first evidence on the returns and risk characteristics of private credit indexes calculated by MSCI, Pitchbook, and Preqin. Broad private credit indexes have outperformed liquid credit markets in both absolute and risk-adjusted terms from 2001 to 2024. We develop a parsimonious two-factor benchmark model based on traded credit and equity factors, demonstrating that this model accounts for almost 90% of the time variation in private credit index returns. Exposure to the equity factor in private credit is significant, suggesting that models based solely on credit factors may overestimate the alpha in private credit. Among credit and equity benchmarks, our analysis indicates that leveraged loans and small-cap value equities provide the greatest explanatory power for the benchmark model, particularly in the more recent post-financial-crisis data. Additionally, we observe variability in the factor exposures and alphas across private credit sub-strategies, indicating that most of the asset class's outperformance is driven by direct lending funds, while opportunistic and asset-backed lending have detracted from the performance of broad indexes.

title:
The Rise of Corporate Sovereignty 
How Big Tech is Reshaping Global Power and Governance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
The Rise of Corporate Sovereignty 
How Big Tech is Reshaping Global Power and Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual/analytical essay and did not involve human participants, patient data, identifiable personal data, or human-subjects research.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding and was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This essay argues that Big Tech companies have evolved into a new class of geopolitical actorscorporate sovereigns-whose authority increasingly rivals or constrains that of nation-states. Their power does not derive from territorial control, but from the ownership and operation of digital infrastructures that have become essential to communication, commerce, administration, and security. Through cloud platforms, identity systems, data pipelines, algorithmic governance, lobbying networks, satellite networks, and AI capabilities, these firms now exercise forms of operational authority once reserved for public institutions. This paper examines how infrastructural dependence, data visibility, economic concentration, political leverage, and security functions collectively produce a form of non-state sovereignty that reshapes global governance. It concludes that the rise of corporate sovereignty marks a structural transformation in the organization of power-one that existing regulatory frameworks cannot fully address, and that demands new philosophical and political models for accountability and democratic oversight.

title: Do Professionals Deliver Better Environmental Outcomes? Evidence from Provincial Environmental Leaders in China (2005–2021)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Do Professionals Deliver Better Environmental Outcomes? Evidence from Provincial Environmental Leaders in China (2005–2021)
detail.abstract: The professionalization of government officials has become a central concern in advancing state capacity and governance effectiveness. Yet, little is known about whether and how professionalized leadership in environmental agencies contributes to environmental performance. Drawing on provincial panel data from China between 2005 and 2021, this study examines the impact of environmental leaders’ professional backgrounds on local environmental outcomes. Using fixed-effects regression models and mediation analysis, the findings reveal that professionalized leaders significantly reduce industrial sulfur dioxide emissions, thereby improving environmental performance. While attention allocation shows no significant mediating effect, administrative enforcement capacity emerges as a robust mediator linking leader professionalization and environmental outcomes. Moreover, the joint presence of attention and enforcement amplifies this mediating effect. Further analysis indicates that before the introduction of the “one-vote veto” system in 2007, social ties moderated the relationship between leader professionalization and environmental performance, but this effect diminished afterward. These results highlight the importance of bureaucratic professionalization for effective environmental governance and suggest that enforcement capacity rather than attention is the key channel. The study contributes to understanding the micro-foundations of environmental governance and provides policy implications for strengthening cadre selection and training in developing countries.

title: Morphological Least Cost Law (MLC Law): A Variational Framework and Empirical Validation

detail.title: Morphological Least Cost Law (MLC Law): A Variational Framework and Empirical Validation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. No human participants or identifiable personal data were used.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This chapter develops a variational-principle-based theory for analyzing asset-price morphology in financial markets-the Morphological Least Cost Law (MLC Law). The objective is to provide a unified, quantifiable, and reproducible structural framework for the evolution of price morphology. We view financial markets as complex adaptive systems, and interpret wave-like price patterns as macroscopic structures that spontaneously emerge from the interactions of countless heterogeneous traders under multiple constraints.
This study delivers three key breakthroughs:
 • Mathematical formalization: the price-morphology problem is formulated as a variational problem in the Sobolev space H²([T0, T1]), and the existence, uniqueness, and C²smoothness of the optimal morphological curve u*(t) are established. 
• Algorithmic proceduralization: a complete translation from theory to algorithm is implemented. By solving the Euler–Lagrange equation via a unified program, Morphological Critical Points (MCPs) are identified objectively, ensuring reproducibility of results. 
• Scientific testing: a falsifiable testing system is constructed based on the residual distribution (goodness-of-fit), counterexample statistics (cases where MCP-based prediction fails), and the interval violation rate (frequency with which price breaks the trend interval).

title: Theoretically assessing blockchain solutions for Zimbabwean Citizens
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Theoretically assessing blockchain solutions for Zimbabwean Citizens
detail.abstract: The founding of Bitcoin (BTC) in 2009, led to the development and establishment of more crypto assets and blockchains. At the time of writing this working paper, the conservative market capitalisation of the crypto asset industry stood at US$ 2.5 trillion; consisting of approximately 12 900 officially registered crypto assets listed on more than 400 officially registered exchanges. It is thus ostensible that individuals who are interested to invest in crypto assets may be overwhelmed with options available to them – stemming from a lack of crypto education. In the same vein, Zimbabwean citizens are advocating for the adoption of Blockchain Technology (BT), yet most of them do not fully understand how this same technology will benefit them. Thus, the primary objectives of this study were to 1) educate the Zimbabwean citizens on the main aspects of BT and 2) to explore the different ways they can benefit from the adoption of BT in Zimbabwe.  To achieve the latter, non-empirical, exploratory research was conducted in the form of an online desktop review. From the research conducted, the main components in BT are 1) the blockchain, 2) crypto assets, 3) crypto exchanges and 4) crypto wallets. In terms of benefits, Zimbabwean citizens can benefit through; 1) increased investment opportunities, 2) convenient, cheap, and fast remittances, 3) business funding opportunities, 4) protection from weakening currency, 5) buying electricity from prosumers, 6) using art to earn income, 7) increased borrowing and lending opportunities, 8) price stability, 9) increased international trade opportunities, 10) improved governance, 11) improved medical services, and 12) improved food services.

title: Factors Influencing the Trading Results of Forex and Crypto Traders in Africa
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Factors Influencing the Trading Results of Forex and Crypto Traders in Africa
detail.abstract: While Crypto Trading (CT) is still gaining momentum, Forex Trading is well established and easily regulated across the world. The success of Bitcoin (BTC), and the development of the Ethereum blockchain, led to the development of a plethora of new coins and tokens. Consequently, traders started to take advantage of the crypto volatility to make a living. Despite the hostility of African governments towards privately crypto assets, CT is gaining momentum. In essence, trading is attractive to Africans because of the high levels of poverty and inequality, as everyone is looking for extra income to survive. However, on average, most traders are failing in their trades. In FT it is generally accepted that more than 90% of traders end up losing their trading investment. Although the failure rate might be low in CT, many traders are still losing money. Hence, the main objectives of this study were to 1) identify the Micro Trading Factors (MicTFs) and Macro Trading Factors (MacTFs) influencing the trading results of African traders and 2) to determine if Artificial Intelligence (AI) can improve the trading results of African traders. To attain these objectives, a non-empirical, exploratory research was conducted in the form of an online desktop review. From the findings, the MicTFs influencing African trading results are patience, emotions, capital, experience, technical analysis, time frames, trading device, fundamental analysis, revenge trading, capital management, overtrading, chart reading, risk management, analysis paralysis, trading plan, and expectations. The MacTFs influencing African trading results are market conditions, lack of electricity, cost of data, and availability of trading platforms. Regarding the use of AI in trading, it was found that African traders, including novice traders, can significantly benefit from using trading robots like Royal Q.

title: The development of Business Seedbed Theories: A permanent solution to poverty and inequality in Africa
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: The development of Business Seedbed Theories: A permanent solution to poverty and inequality in Africa
detail.abstract: Because of their job creation potential, Small Businesses (SBs) are key to the reduction of poverty and inequality across the world.  In an African dispensation, SBs are regarded as the engine for economic growth. In essence, these business entities account for more than 75% of African enterprises. Despite the significant number of African SBs, the continent is still plagued with high levels of poverty and inequality, mainly because of weak business sustainability of African SBs. Previous studies identified many reasons for this weak sustainability, and these include stiff competition, lack of capital, unstable electricity supply, high electricity costs, high crime rate, and high inflation rates. To improve the African SBs’ sustainability, the main objectives of this study were to; 1) develop new theories that will foster business sustainability in Africa and 2) discuss the use of the developed theories in Private Cities (PCs). To attain these objectives, a non-empirical, exploratory research was conducted in the form of an online desktop review. From the study, three Business Seedbed Theories (BSTs) were developed using the concepts of interdependence, cooperation, business ecosystem, Group Companies, and PCs. Furthermore, it was found that PCs play a crucial role in enhancing the sustainability of SBs, due to 1) lack of competition at the early business development stages and 2) enhanced economic environment.

title: Universal Money Instrument Decentralised Finance vs Ethereum Decentralised Finance: The Quest of Goliath and David to Conquer Africa.
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Universal Money Instrument Decentralised Finance vs Ethereum Decentralised Finance: The Quest of Goliath and David to Conquer Africa.
detail.abstract: Few years after the development of Bitcoin (BTC), there was need to develop another blockchain that could support many applications, and consequently, the Ethereum Blockchain (EB) was developed. One of the key initiatives that was enabled by the development of the EB is that of Decentralised Finance (DeFi). Understanding the massive potential of DeFi, particularly in developing markets, many other developers are embarking on projects to develop their DeFi supporting blockchains. The Universal Money Instrument (UMI) team is one of the groups that embarked on this journey. Approximately 1.5 years after the launch of the UMI Blockchain (UMI B) and the UMI coin, the team recently released their DeFi manifest. Considering that Africa stands to benefit more from DeFi, it is expected that these two blockchains will compete for dominance in Africa. Hence, the main objective of this study was to determine the most suitable blockchain for the African continent. To achieve the above objective, a non-empirical, exploratory research was conducted in the form of an online desktop review. It was found that the UMI DeFi is ideal for Africa because the UMI B; is highly scalable, supports nearinstant transactions, offers free transactions, uses a superior consensus algorithm, took longer to develop, and safe from attacks like the 51% attacks.

title: Children, Digital Identity, and Manipulative Design: Tort Law Responses to Data Exploitation and Behavioural Profiling in Algorithmic Advertising Ecosystems
